name: Cambodian Genocide / Khmer Rouge
description: The Cambodian Genocide (1975-1979) was perpetrated by the Khmer Rouge regime under Pol Pot, resulting in the deaths of approximately 1.7-2 million people—roughly 25% of Cambodia's population. Victims included intellectuals, ethnic minorities, and political opponents, killed through executions, forced labor, and starvation.
hook: The Khmer Rouge's 'Year Zero' killed 1.7-2 million Cambodians—a quarter of the population—in the 1970s genocide.
narrative: Pol Pot's Khmer Rouge took power (1975) and implemented radical social engineering. Cities were emptied; intellectuals were executed; peasants were enslaved in labor camps. Ethnic minorities (Vietnamese, Chinese, Thai, Chams) faced extermination. Starvation killed as many as execution. By 1979, Vietnam invaded and ended the regime. Estimates: 1.7-2 million died (1975-1979). The Khmer Rouge Tribunal eventually tried surviving leaders, but decades passed before justice.
significance: The Cambodian genocide became the modern template for genocide prosecution. The delayed tribunal showed that international justice could still occur decades later. Survivor trauma shaped Cambodian society; many fled as refugees. The genocide's ideological blend of Maoism and Khmer nationalism influenced postwar Cambodian politics. Modern Cambodia memorializes genocide victims; education about atrocities is emphasized. The genocide remains traumatic for survivors and shapes Cambodia's international standing.

name: Afghan-Soviet War Extended
description: Ten-year Soviet invasion establishing communist rule.

casualtyRange.notes: Soviet military ~15k; Afghan military ~20k; civilians 500k-2M (highly disputed). Mujahideen claims reach 3M+.

hook: A decade-long Soviet occupation of Afghanistan created a quagmire that weakened the USSR and destabilized Central Asia.
narrative: In 1979, the Soviet Union invaded Afghanistan to support a communist regime facing Islamic resistance. Soviet forces, numbering over 100,000, faced Afghan mujahideen fighters armed by the United States, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan. The conflict became a Cold War proxy war, with U.S. weapons (including Stinger missiles) inflicting heavy losses on Soviet helicopters and armor. Soviet forces controlled major cities but could not suppress rural insurgency. The war devastated Afghanistan: 1-2 million deaths, 5 million refugees, and infrastructure destruction. Soviet troops suffered 15,000 deaths; withdrawal began in 1988 and completed in 1989. The conflict contributed significantly to the Soviet Union's economic collapse.
significance: The Afghan War became the Soviet Union's 'Vietnam,' draining resources and contributing to its collapse in 1991. The conflict strengthened Islamic militancy and created bases for future terrorism (Taliban, Al Qaeda). The U.S. support for mujahideen had long-term blowback consequences. The war destabilized Central Asia and demonstrated the limits of conventional military power against irregular insurgency.

name: Soviet-Afghan War
description: Soviet invasion and occupation resisted by Mujahideen with US support, contributing to Soviet collapse.
hook: Soviet invasion of Afghanistan triggered a prolonged guerrilla war that hastened the USSR's decline.
narrative: The Soviet invasion (December 1979) aimed to prop up a communist regime under threat from Islamic insurgents. Soviet forces included 85,000 troops initially, later increased to 120,000. Major operations targeted mujahideen strongholds in rural areas, including the Panjshir Valley (repeatedly attacked but never fully conquered). U.S. CIA support provided mujahideen with modern weapons, including Stinger anti-aircraft missiles (1986) that devastated Soviet air superiority. Soviet tactics—helicopter gunships, massive bombing campaigns, civilian relocation—caused enormous destruction. Withdrawal began in 1988; the last Soviet troops left in February 1989. Over 50,000 Soviet soldiers died; Afghan casualties exceeded 1 million.
significance: The Afghan War became symbolic of Soviet overreach and contributed to the Cold War's end. The war demonstrated the ineffectiveness of conventional military power against insurgency motivated by religious ideology and nationalist fervor. The U.S. investment in the mujahideen had long-term consequences, including the rise of the Taliban and Al Qaeda. The war's legacy includes Afghanistan's destabilization and Central Asia's strategic importance in post-Cold War geopolitics.

casualtyRange.notes: 1979-1989; Afghan civilians heavily affected

hook: An 8-year war between two OPEC powers killed 500,000-1 million and destabilized the Middle East.
narrative: The Iran-Iraq War (1980-1988) erupted when Iraq, under Saddam Hussein, invaded Iran to capture oil-rich territories. Iraqi forces achieved initial success but encountered fierce Iranian resistance. The war deteriorated into a brutal stalemate with massive casualties on both sides. Both nations used chemical weapons extensively; Iraq employed them against civilian targets (particularly the Kurdish enclave). The war featured massive tank battles reminiscent of World War II, as well as human-wave infantry assaults by Iranian Revolutionary Guards. International intervention (U.S. support for Iraq, Soviet arms to both sides) complicated the conflict. A UN-brokered ceasefire (1988) ended the war without territorial changes.
significance: The Iran-Iraq War killed 500,000-1 million people and destroyed both nations' economies. The war demonstrated the devastating potential of modern warfare when combined with ideological fervor and chemical weapons. The conflict established Saddam Hussein as a key regional actor and emboldened his subsequent invasion of Kuwait (1990). The war's aftermath left Iran and Iraq weakened, enabling subsequent Israeli and Western military dominance in the region. The conflict highlighted the international community's failure to enforce chemical weapons conventions.

hook: North-South civil war killed 2 million—Africa's costliest conflict—and nearly tore the African continent's largest nation apart.
narrative: Sudan's 1983-2005 civil war pitted the Arabized Muslim north against the Christian and animist south. Southern rebels (SPLA) fought the Khartoum government's Arabization and Islamization policies. The war devastated the south with famines that killed hundreds of thousands beyond combat deaths. Oil reserves and religious ideology deepened the conflict. A 2005 peace deal granted the south autonomy and a referendum, which led to South Sudan's independence in 2011—Africa's newest nation. Over 2 million died; millions more were displaced.
significance: The war created an independence movement that redrew Africa's map. South Sudan's birth was celebrated globally but quickly descended into post-conflict violence. The original conflict exposed how colonial legacies (north-south divides) and resource competition fuel enduring wars. Sudan's strategy of weaponizing famine became a model study in humanitarian crises.

name: Sudanese Civil War
description: Long civil war resulting in South Sudanese independence and regional destabilization.
hook: Africa's longest civil war devastated Sudan for 22 years, killing over 2 million and shaping African politics.
narrative: Sudan's civil war (1983-2005) pitted the Islamic government in the north against the SPLA (Sudan People's Liberation Army) representing the Christian and animist south. The conflict was rooted in colonial-era divisions: Arab-Islamic north versus African south. The government deployed chemical weapons, napalm, and military planes; the SPLA used guerrilla tactics. Famine became a weapon; the government restricted food aid to rebel areas. The UN estimated 2 million deaths; many from starvation. The conflict destabilized the entire region, affecting Ethiopia, Uganda, and Kenya. The U.S. supported the SPLA; foreign powers (China, Saudi Arabia) supported the government. The Comprehensive Peace Agreement (2005) ended the war and established South Sudan's path to independence (2011).
significance: The Sudanese Civil War was Africa's deadliest conflict of the post-Cold War era. The conflict's outcome established the principle of southern Sudan's self-determination and led to Africa's newest nation-state (South Sudan). The war's famine exposed the inadequacy of international humanitarian responses. The conflict influenced African Union policy on internal conflicts. Sudan's subsequent divisions continue to shape East African geopolitics.

name: Gulf War
description: US-led coalition war evicting Iraqi forces from Kuwait establishing American regional dominance.
hook: Iraq's invasion of Kuwait (1990) triggered a US-led coalition war that liberated Kuwait but left Saddam in power.
narrative: Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein invaded Kuwait (Aug 1990) for its oil and territory. US, EU, and Arab states formed a coalition to liberate Kuwait. Air campaign (Jan-Feb 1991) devastated Iraqi military and infrastructure. Ground campaign (Feb 1991) lasted 100 hours; coalition forces routed Iraqi forces. Kuwait was liberated; Iraq's military was shattered. Approximately 25,000-200,000 Iraqis died (estimates vary widely); 300+ coalition soldiers died. Saddam remained in power; US refrained from marching to Baghdad. Post-war sanctions severely damaged Iraqi economy and civilian population.
significance: The Gulf War was the first major post-Cold War conflict and demonstrated US military dominance. The war showed the effectiveness of precision air power (though civilian casualties were high). The war established a US-led international order and showcased the UN Security Council's ability to authorize force. However, leaving Saddam in power allowed him to suppress Shia and Kurdish uprisings brutally. Post-war sanctions (Iraq War Syndrome) killed 500,000+ Iraqi children according to some estimates—a humanitarian catastrophe. The war planted seeds for the 2003 Iraq War; unresolved tensions in Iraq persisted. The war established the Middle East as a primary arena for US military intervention, beginning the 'War on Terror' that would define 21st-century US foreign policy.

name: Rwandan Civil War and Genocide
description: Civil war escalating into genocide of Tutsi and moderate Hutu populations, resulting in approximately one million deaths over 100 days and becoming a defining tragedy of the post-Cold War period.

casualtyRange.notes: 1994 genocide plus civil war context. Estimates ~800k widely cited. Rapid genocide over ~100 days.

hook: In 100 days, Hutus massacred 800,000 Tutsis with machetes and improvised weapons while the world watched.
narrative: Rwanda's 1994 genocide erupted after a Hutu extremist shot down President Juvénal Habyarimana's plane in April. Within hours, Hutu militias and ordinary citizens began systematically hunting Tutsis and moderate Hutus. Local broadcasters incited killings while roadblocks separated victims by ethnicity. Neighboring Tutsi forces under Paul Kagame fought back, eventually halting the genocide by July. Estimates suggest 800,000 to 1 million people died in the fastest mass slaughter of the 20th century. Roughly 2 million Hutus fled Rwanda as Kagame's army advanced, creating a humanitarian crisis across Central Africa.
significance: The genocide shattered international peacekeeping doctrine and exposed the UN's inability to prevent atrocities. It led to the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda—the first modern tribunal prosecuting genocide. Today, Rwanda's recovery model and Kagame's authoritarian stability represent both post-conflict resilience and contested justice. The genocide fundamentally changed how the world thinks about humanitarian intervention and the phrase 'never again' has become hollow to many.

name: Yugoslav Wars
description: Series of ethnic conflicts following Yugoslavia's dissolution resulting in independent Balkan states.
hook: Communist Yugoslavia's violent dissolution (1991-1999) created multiple wars, ethnic cleansing, and NATO's first European bombing campaign.
narrative: After Tito's death, Yugoslav federation fragmented. Slovenia (1991) and Croatia (1991-1995) seceded relatively quickly, though Croatia's war was brutal. Macedonia (1991) left peacefully. Bosnia-Herzegovina (1992-1995) saw genocidal conflict (see Bosnian War). Kosovo (1998-1999) saw Serbian forces attacked Albanian population; NATO bombed Serbia (first bombing of European sovereign state). The wars killed roughly 250,000; 2-3 million were displaced. The Yugoslav wars fragmented the federation into seven nations (Slovenia, Croatia, Serbia, Montenegro, Bosnia, Macedonia, Kosovo). The wars were Europe's bloodiest since WWII.
significance: Yugoslav wars ended communism's façade of unified brotherhood. They demonstrated ethnic nationalism's power in post-Cold War politics. The wars prompted NATO's expansion (eastward) and international intervention doctrine. They established the principle that NATO could intervene in sovereign states for humanitarian reasons (a contentious precedent). The wars shaped post-Cold War European identity—Eastern European states sought NATO membership and EU integration. The wars demonstrated that Europe's ethnic diversity could explode into violence when authoritarian order collapsed. Modern Eastern European NATO members often cite Yugoslav wars as justification for military alliance against Russia. The wars remain traumatic for Balkans' populations and shape regional politics.

name: Bosnian War
description: Ethnic conflict in Bosnia featuring genocide, ethnic cleansing, and international intervention.
hook: Yugoslavia's collapse sparked Balkan genocide (1992-1995): Serbs, Croats, and Bosniaks fought for territory; 100,000+ died.
narrative: Yugoslavia's communist federation fragmented after Tito's death (1980). Nationalistic movements in Slovenia, Croatia, and Bosnia-Herzegovina sought independence. Serbs (largest ethnic group) resisted fragmentation. Slovenia's independence war (1991) was brief; Croatia's was brutal (1991-1995). Bosnia's was catastrophic (1992-1995): Serbs, Croats, and Bosniaks (Muslim Bosnians) fought for control. Bosnian Serbs, supported by Serbia's Milosevic, conducted ethnic cleansing of Bosniaks. The Srebrenica massacre (1995) killed 8,000+ Bosniaks. NATO intervention (1995) halted the war. Roughly 100,000 died; 2 million were displaced.
significance: The Bosnian War shattered the post-Cold War dream of universal peace. It showed that ethnic nationalism could fuel genocide in Europe in the 1990s. The war prompted NATO's expansion and intervention doctrine. The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia prosecuted war crimes—establishing precedent for ICC. Srebrenica became emblematic of UN/NATO failure to prevent genocide (similar to Rwanda). The war demonstrated that Balkan tensions, suppressed under communism, exploded when repression ended. Bosnian Muslims' refugee crisis prompted international rethinking of asylum and humanitarian intervention. Modern Bosnia remains ethnically divided with international oversight—a fractured post-conflict state.

name: Rwandan Genocide
description: Genocidal massacre of Tutsi and moderate Hutu by Hutu extremists in 100 days.

casualtyRange.notes: Widely cited as ~800k. Tutsi estimates 500-1M. Rapid genocide over ~100 days (April-June 1994).

hook: In 100 days, Hutu militias killed approximately 1 million Tutsis in one of history's fastest genocides.
narrative: The Rwandan Genocide (April-July 1994) was triggered by the assassination of President Habyarimana. Within hours, Hutu militias began systematic massacres of Tutsis and moderate Hutus. Armed Interahamwe and Impuzamugambi militias, often organized by local officials and clergy, executed mass killings. The genocide was methodical: killers used machetes, clubs with nails, and firearms. Entire families were murdered in homes, churches, and schools. The UN Security Council, dominated by powerful nations, reduced the UN peacekeeping force from 2,500 to 270 troops, crippling the ability to stop the genocide. The International Committee of the Red Cross, journalists, and some NGOs documented the atrocities. The Rwandan Patriotic Front's military victory and invasion stopped the genocide but could not prevent approximately 800,000-1,000,000 deaths.
significance: The Rwandan Genocide was one of the fastest and most complete genocides relative to population. The genocide exposed the international community's unwillingness to intervene in African conflicts despite evidence of mass atrocities. The genocide prompted the creation of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, advancing international justice mechanisms. Rwanda's post-genocide reconciliation efforts (Truth and Reconciliation Commission) influenced subsequent post-conflict justice processes. The genocide's aftermath shaped international norms about the 'Responsibility to Protect' and humanitarian intervention.

hook: Regional powers and foreign interests fought for control of the mineral-rich Democratic Republic of Congo.
narrative: After the 1994 Rwandan genocide, Hutu militias fled into eastern Congo. Rwanda and Uganda invaded (1996) to pursue the militias, toppling dictator Mobutu in 1997. Laurent-Désiré Kabila took power but clashed with his former allies. In 1998, Rwanda, Uganda, Burundi, Angola, and other regional powers invaded Congo, seeking mineral wealth and political leverage. The war lasted until 2003, involving nine nations directly. South Africa, Zimbabwe, Namibia, and Chad intervened on various sides. The conflict killed an estimated 2.5-5.4 million people, mostly from disease and starvation. Peace agreements (1999, 2002) established a transitional government and UN mission.
significance: The Second Congo War devastated Central Africa's most resource-rich nation and became one of the deadliest conflicts since World War II. It highlighted the role of regional powers in African conflicts, the impact of the Rwandan genocide's spillover, and the international community's limited capacity to prevent mass death. The war's legacy includes ongoing instability in eastern Congo and mineral supply chain debates.

name: War on Terror/Al-Qaeda Conflict

hook: A decentralized global conflict against terrorism spawned two major wars, surveillance expansions, and ongoing instability.
narrative: The War on Terror began after Al-Qaeda's attacks on the United States (September 11, 2001), which killed nearly 3,000 people. The U.S. invaded Afghanistan (October 2001) to pursue Al-Qaeda and overthrow the Taliban regime harboring them. The Afghanistan War lasted until 2021. Subsequently, the U.S. invaded Iraq (2003), claiming weapons of mass destruction, toppling Saddam Hussein's regime. The Iraq War (2003-2011, with U.S. troops returning 2014-2017) killed hundreds of thousands and destabilized the region. The conflict expanded globally: U.S. drone strikes in Yemen, Pakistan, Somalia; military operations in Syria; and intelligence operations worldwide. The wars cost over 2 trillion dollars and killed approximately 500,000-1 million people directly and indirectly.
significance: The War on Terror became the defining conflict of the early 21st century, reshaping international relations and U.S. foreign policy. The wars in Afghanistan and Iraq failed to achieve stated objectives and instead destabilized the Middle East. The conflict enabled the rise of ISIS (Islamic State) and other terrorist organizations. The War on Terror justified unprecedented surveillance and security measures, expanding state power globally. The wars' costs contributed to economic challenges for the U.S. and shifted global power dynamics toward rising powers like China.

name: War in Afghanistan (2001-2021)

hook: A 20-year American war in Afghanistan ultimately ended in defeat and Taliban return to power.
narrative: The War in Afghanistan (2001-2021) began with the U.S. invasion to pursue Al-Qaeda and overthrow the Taliban. Initial U.S. military success quickly defeated Taliban forces and established a U.S.-backed government. However, the Taliban regrouped and waged a persistent insurgency. The war gradually escalated, with NATO allies (Britain, Germany, Canada, Australia) deploying forces. U.S. troop levels peaked at 100,000 (2010-2011). The war involved counterinsurgency operations, drone strikes, and attempts to build Afghan military and government capacity. Despite two decades of effort and $2 trillion spent, the Taliban remained effective. U.S. withdrawal accelerated under Trump and Biden administrations. By August 2021, the Taliban conquered the capital Kabul and re-established control over Afghanistan.
significance: The Afghanistan War demonstrated the limits of U.S. military power against determined insurgency motivated by nationalist and religious fervor. The war's failure undermined U.S. credibility and revealed overconfidence in military solutions to political problems. The Taliban's victory validated arguments about avoiding long-term military interventions in complex political environments. The war's end enabled the U.S. to focus on China as the primary strategic competitor. Afghanistan's return to Taliban control disrupted U.S. strategy in Asia and enabled the Taliban to provide safe haven to various militant groups.

hook: Boko Haram's insurgency (2009-present) in northern Nigeria killed 40,000+, displaced 2+ million, and destabilized West Africa.
narrative: Boko Haram, an Islamic extremist group, emerged in northern Nigeria (2009) opposing Western education and demanding Islamic governance. The group conducted bombings, massacres, and kidnappings (notably 276 schoolgirls in 2014). Nigerian military response was brutal, with alleged extrajudicial killings. The conflict spread to Niger, Chad, and Cameroon. By 2023, Boko Haram fractured into splinter groups. Estimates: 40,000+ killed; 2+ million displaced; thousands of schoolchildren abducted.
significance: Boko Haram showed how extremist ideologies could mobilize populations in economically marginalized regions. The group's kidnapping of schoolgirls created international outcry (Bring Back Our Girls movement). The conflict demonstrated state military's difficulty combating asymmetric terrorism in ungoverned spaces. The conflict destabilized the Sahel and fueled extremism across West Africa. Modern West Africa faces ongoing terrorism and state fragmentation linked to Boko Haram's conflicts.

hook: Syrian uprising (2011) became a devastating civil war, killing 500,000+, displacing 13 million, and destabilizing the entire region.
narrative: Arab Spring protests reached Syria (March 2011) against President Bashar al-Assad's authoritarian rule. Assad's forces brutally suppressed protests, sparking armed rebellion. Civil war escalated into complex multi-sided conflict: government forces, various rebel factions, ISIS, Kurdish forces, and foreign interventions (Russia, Iran, US). The war devastated Syria: entire cities were destroyed, chemical weapons were used against civilians, civilians faced starvation, and millions fled as refugees. By 2023, the war continues with no resolution. Estimates: 500,000-600,000 dead; 13+ million displaced (refugees and internally displaced).
significance: The Syrian civil war is the 21st century's deadliest conflict and shows how sectarian, geopolitical, and foreign interventions can escalate civil conflict. The war demonstrated Russia's willingness to militarily support autocratic allies. The war's refugee crisis (5+ million to Turkey, Lebanon, Jordan) destabilized neighboring countries and influenced European politics (resurgent right-wing movements blamed refugees). The war showed how barrel bombs, chemical weapons, and starvation can be used as weapons of war without international intervention. The humanitarian toll is catastrophic; reconstruction will take decades. The war's unresolved status (Assad nominally victorious but Syria fractured) shows that military victory doesn't restore state capacity or resolve underlying conflicts. Modern Syria remains a failed state.

name: ISIS in Iraq and Syria
description: Five-year war against ISIS caliphate.
hook: ISIS (ISIL) conquered Iraq and Syria (2014-2017), killing hundreds of thousands and creating the worst humanitarian crisis of the 21st century.
narrative: Islamic State (ISIS/ISIL) emerged from Iraqi insurgency remnants. By 2014, ISIS controlled large swaths of Iraq and Syria. ISIS used extreme violence (beheadings, slavery, massacres) to terrify and control populations. The group exploited sectarian tensions, Iraq's state weakness, and Syria's civil war. ISIS attracted foreign fighters (20,000+) from around the world. A US-led coalition counterattack (2017) gradually degraded ISIS militarily. Estimates: hundreds of thousands killed by ISIS and in counter-operations; 10+ million displaced. Yazidis, Christians, and Shias were targeted for genocide.
significance: ISIS represented a new form of transnational terrorism and proto-state organization. The group's social media recruitment showed modern radicalization tactics. ISIS's defeat (2017) did not eliminate the ideology or organization. ISIS prisoners and fighters remain detained; the group maintains presence in fragmented form. The conflict's humanitarian toll is still being assessed; trauma and displacement will affect generations. The conflict demonstrated that extremist groups could exploit state failure to build territorial control. Modern terrorism strategies often invoke ISIS as model or deterrent.

narrative: Yemen's government collapse and Houthi insurgency triggered civil war (2015). Saudi Arabia and UAE launched air campaign supporting government forces. Saudi bombing killed civilians indiscriminately; blockade created famine. Houthis used drones and missiles. Multiple factions fought; ISIS and Al-Qaeda exploited chaos. By 2023, the war continues with no resolution. Estimates: 500,000+ deaths (mostly starvation); 30+ million people food insecure. Yemen is a humanitarian catastrophe.
significance: Yemen's war is the world's worst humanitarian crisis per UN. Saudi involvement and US weapons transfers raised international moral questions. The blockade's use as a weapon of war showed sophisticated use of economic strangulation. The war demonstrates how regional conflicts become geopolitical proxies (Iran supports Houthis; Saudi-UAE support government). The humanitarian scale—30 million food-insecure—approaches failure of humanitarian systems. Modern Yemen remains a failed state with immense suffering.

Tens of thousands have been killed and over 700,000 have fled to Bangladesh. The UN has documented evidence of genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes.
hook: Myanmar's military campaign (2016-present) against stateless Rohingya Muslims killed 25,000+, displaced 750,000, and constitutes genocide.
narrative: Myanmar's military targeted the Rohingya, a Muslim ethnic minority denied citizenship. Military operations (2016-2017) were brutal: villages were burned, civilians massacred, sexual violence systematized. Over 750,000 Rohingya fled to Bangladesh, creating the world's largest refugee camp (Cox's Bazar). International investigations documented genocide. Aung San Suu Kyi, celebrated democracy icon, defended the military's actions—damaging her reputation. The military junta remained in power despite international pressure. Estimates: 25,000+ killed directly; disease and starvation added to deaths. Rohingya remain stateless.
significance: The Rohingya genocide showed that 21st-century genocides persist despite international law. Myanmar's military escaped accountability; Western countries levied limited sanctions. The genocide demonstrated that even celebrated democrats (Aung San Suu Kyi) could defend atrocities. The refugee crisis destabilized Bangladesh and raised questions about responsibility-sharing. The genocide's minimal military intervention (unlike Libya 2011) showed inconsistency in humanitarian intervention doctrine. The Rohingya remain essentially trapped as perpetual refugees—a humanitarian tragedy. The genocide is ongoing in low-intensity form; Rohingya trapped in camps face disease and violence.

name: Tigray War
description: Major conflict between Ethiopian federal forces and the TPLF in Tigray region, causing humanitarian crisis with mass atrocities, mass starvation, and mass displacement.

casualtyRange.notes: Ghent University estimates 300,000-600,000 incl. famine; battlefield deaths ~160,000+

hook: Ethiopia's Tigray War (2020-2022) killed 500,000+ through combat, famine, and sexual violence—Africa's deadliest recent conflict.
narrative: Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed ordered military operations against the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) over governance disputes. The conflict escalated into ethnic violence targeting Tigrayans. Ethiopian and Eritrean forces used starvation, sexual violence, and massacre as tactics. Humanitarian access was blocked; millions faced famine. The conflict displaced 2+ million. Both sides committed atrocities. International humanitarian organizations documented war crimes. By 2022, a ceasefire was reached, though it remains fragile. Estimates: 600,000+ deaths (mostly from starvation and massacre).
significance: The Tigray War is 21st century's deadliest conflict by official counts, yet received minimal international media coverage compared to Ukraine. The conflict demonstrated how ethnic nationalism and state power can produce genocide. Sexual violence was systematized as a weapon of war. The conflict showed how Nobel Peace Prize can be premature and how authoritarian leaders can win international sympathy temporarily. The war's minimal international response compared to Ukraine highlights global inequality in conflict attention and intervention. Tigray humanitarian crisis is ongoing; reconstruction is years away. The conflict is Africa's worst humanitarian disaster; global indifference is damning.

Total casualties including the wounded exceed 1M for Russia and several hundred thousand for Ukraine. UN-verified civilian deaths ~14,000, believed to be an undercount. All figures are estimates and disputed.

hook: Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine has killed hundreds of thousands of soldiers on both sides, displaced 8+ million people, and triggered the largest European war since 1945.
narrative: Russia invaded Ukraine (Feb 2022) seeking regime change and territorial control. Ukraine resisted fiercely; President Zelensky became a symbol of defiance. Atrocities emerged: Bucha massacre, Irpin killings, sexual violence. Russia withdrew from Kiev (March 2022) but consolidated control in Donbas. Artillery-heavy war of attrition followed. NATO supplied weapons; Ukraine received military aid worth tens of billions. By 2025, the war continued with no resolution. Casualty figures are contested, but every credible estimate finds Russian losses substantially higher than Ukrainian. Military deaths (distinct from total casualties, which also count the wounded) are put at roughly 150,000-250,000 for Russia (UK Ministry of Defence and CSIS, 2025) against roughly 45,000-100,000 for Ukraine (President Zelensky cited about 43,000 killed in December 2024; several Western estimates run higher). Counting the wounded, total casualties exceed one million for Russia and several hundred thousand for Ukraine. The UN has verified about 14,000 civilian deaths, with the true toll believed to be considerably higher. More than 8 million Ukrainians were displaced.
significance: Russia's invasion shattered the post-Cold War international order and triggered NATO's largest expansion since Cold War. The war revived European militarization and defense spending. Ukrainian resistance inspired global sympathy and demonstrated smaller nations' capacity to resist. The war's scale (Eastern Front) became the largest European conflict since WWII. Western military aid to Ukraine (weapons, intelligence) became central to conflict. Russia's isolation accelerated its dependence on China. The war remains unresolved; the potential for wider NATO-Russia conflict remains.

hook: Israel's 2023 war in Gaza following Hamas attack killed 40,000+ Palestinians, destroyed cities, and created humanitarian catastrophe.
narrative: Hamas launched surprise attack on Israel (Oct 7, 2023), killing 1,200 Israelis and taking hostages. Israel responded with massive airstrikes on Gaza, killing Palestinian civilians indiscriminately. Ground invasion followed; Israel conquered Gaza territory. The war devastated Gaza: 40,000+ Palestinians killed (mostly civilians); 2+ million displaced; cities destroyed; humanitarian system collapsed. International condemnation increased; ceasefire negotiations were prolonged.
significance: The Gaza War showed the human cost of modern urban warfare. The conflict's death toll and humanitarian crisis created international outcry. Israel-Hamas conflict remains unresolved; Gaza's future status is contested. The war influenced global politics (protests, political divisions) and Israeli-Palestinian stalemate seems permanent. The war showed how occupied populations' desperate rebellion sparks disproportionate military response.

Iran launched 300+ drones and missiles at Israel; most were intercepted. Israel struck Iranian military targets. Escalation raised fears of wider regional war and nuclear confrontation. As of 2024, tensions remain high with ongoing threats of further attacks. Limited direct combat deaths but enormous symbolic significance.
significance: The 2024 conflict marked Iran-Israel tensions' escalation from proxy wars to direct military exchanges. It demonstrated international weapons systems' sophistication (air defenses). The conflict raised fears of wider Middle Eastern war involving US, Israel, Iran, and potentially nuclear weapons. The conflict's resolution remains uncertain; de-escalation is unclear. Modern Middle East geopolitics are shaped by Iran-Israel antagonism; nuclear weapons make direct conflict catastrophic.

casualtyRange.notes: Over 1,000 Athenians killed and ~2,000 captured; the Theban Sacred Band was annihilated (254 of 300 fell). Total figures approximate.

description: Philip II of Macedon, with his son Alexander commanding a wing, crushed a coalition of Greek city-states led by Athens and Thebes in Boeotia. The victory established Macedonian hegemony over Greece and ended the era of the independent Greek polis.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Chaeronea (338 BC)
Livius.org (Jona Lendering)

name: Battle of Mantinea (362 BC)

casualtyRange.notes: Diodorus gives c. 1,000 Theban and 4,000 allied dead; modern scholars favour roughly 300-500 per side. The decisive loss was Epaminondas himself.

description: The largest hoplite battle fought among Greek states, in which the Theban general Epaminondas defeated a Spartan-led coalition using his oblique-order tactics but was mortally wounded. His death left a power vacuum that paved the way for Macedonian ascendancy.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Mantinea (362 BC)
Britannica: Battle of Mantineia

name: Battle of Cynoscephalae

casualtyRange.notes: Roman casualties ~700; Macedonians reportedly lost ~8,000 killed and ~5,000 captured. Ancient figures, treated cautiously.

description: Titus Quinctius Flamininus's Roman-Aetolian army defeated Philip V of Macedon in Thessaly during the Second Macedonian War, demonstrating the flexibility of the Roman manipular legion against the Macedonian phalanx on broken ground. The battle ended the war and established Roman influence over Greece.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Cynoscephalae
Livius.org (Jona Lendering)

name: Battle of Magnesia
locations: Magnesia ad Sipylum, Lydia (modern Manisa, Turkey)
countries: Roman Republic and Kingdom of Pergamon

casualtyRange.notes: Modern estimates: ~10,000 Seleucid and ~5,000 Roman-Pergamene dead. Ancient sources claim up to 50,000 Seleucid dead (two thirds of the army).

description: A Roman-Pergamene army under Lucius Cornelius Scipio Asiaticus and Eumenes II decisively defeated the much larger Seleucid army of Antiochus III the Great in Lydia during the Roman-Seleucid War. The defeat led to the Treaty of Apamea and ended Seleucid power in Asia Minor.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Magnesia
Britannica: Battle of Magnesia

name: Battle of Pydna
locations: Plain south of Pydna, Macedonia, Greece

casualtyRange.notes: Roman losses minimal (~100 killed); Macedonians reportedly lost over 20,000 killed and ~6,000 captured. Ancient figures, treated cautiously.

description: Lucius Aemilius Paullus's Roman army annihilated the Macedonian phalanx of King Perseus in the Third Macedonian War, ending the Antigonid dynasty and Macedonian independence. The battle is a classic demonstration of the legion's adaptability over the phalanx once its formation was broken.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Pydna
Britannica: Battle of Pydna

name: Battle of the Allia
locations: Confluence of the Allia brook and Tiber, north of Rome, Italy

casualtyRange.notes: Ancient figures unreliable / no reliable estimate. Accounts written centuries later; Roman tradition dates the battle 390 BC, modern historians often favour 387 BC.

description: A Gallic army of the Senones under Brennus routed the Roman army at the Allia brook and went on to sack Rome itself. The day (dies Alliensis) was thereafter regarded as ill-omened in the Roman calendar.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of the Allia
World History Encyclopedia

name: Battle of Aquae Sextiae

casualtyRange.notes: Romans claimed ~90,000 killed and ~20,000 captured; the Teutones and Ambrones were effectively destroyed. Figures are Roman claims and almost certainly inflated.

description: Gaius Marius destroyed the migrating Teutones and Ambrones near Aquae Sextiae in southern Gaul, reversing a string of earlier Roman disasters in the Cimbrian War. The victory helped cement Marius's reputation and his reformed legions.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Aquae Sextiae
History of War

name: Battle of Vercellae
locations: Raudine Plain near Vercellae, Cisalpine Gaul (northern Italy)

casualtyRange.notes: Romans claimed 65,000-160,000 Cimbri killed and ~60,000 captured; the Cimbri were virtually annihilated. Figures are ancient claims and likely exaggerated.

description: Gaius Marius and Quintus Lutatius Catulus annihilated the Cimbri on the Raudine Plain in northern Italy, ending the Cimbrian War and the Germanic-Celtic threat to Italy. The victory made Marius the foremost Roman of his day.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Vercellae
History of War

name: Battle of Mobei
locations: North of the Gobi Desert, Mongolian Plateau

casualtyRange.notes: Chinese records claim ~19,000-90,000 Xiongnu killed or captured across the two columns; Han forces suffered heavy losses too. Figures from Han chronicles, treated cautiously.

description: A massive Han offensive of around 100,000 cavalry under Wei Qing and Huo Qubing struck deep beyond the Gobi Desert against the Xiongnu Chanyu's main forces. The campaign broke Xiongnu power on the northern frontier and removed the immediate threat to Han China for a generation.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Mobei

name: Seleucid-Mauryan War
locations: Indus Valley and the eastern Iranian/Afghan borderlands

casualtyRange.notes: Ancient figures unreliable / no reliable estimate. It is uncertain whether a pitched battle even occurred; sources record only the settlement.

description: Seleucus I Nicator crossed the Indus into the former eastern satrapies of Alexander's empire and confronted Chandragupta Maurya. sources.label: Wikipedia: Seleucid-Mauryan war

name: Battle of Issus
locations: Plain of Issus near the Pinarus River, Cilicia (modern Turkey)

casualtyRange.notes: Macedonian dead estimated low (hundreds to ~7,000 wounded); Persian dead reported by ancient writers as enormous (tens of thousands, some claims up to 100,000). Ancient figures highly exaggerated.

description: Alexander the Great defeated Darius III in person at Issus, in a narrow coastal plain in Cilicia where Persian numbers could not be brought to bear. Darius fled, abandoning his family, and the victory opened the Levant and Egypt to Macedonian conquest.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Issus

name: Battle of the Eurymedon
locations: Mouth of the Eurymedon River, Pamphylia (southern Anatolia)

casualtyRange.notes: Ancient figures unreliable / no reliable estimate. Exact date (c. 469-466 BC) and casualty totals are uncertain.

description: Cimon of Athens led the Delian League to a double victory on land and sea over Persian forces at the mouth of the Eurymedon River in Pamphylia. The victory broke Persian naval power in the eastern Mediterranean and consolidated Athenian dominance in the Aegean.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of the Eurymedon
Britannica: Cimon

name: Battle of Plataea

casualtyRange.notes: Herodotus claims only ~159 Greek and over 250,000 Persian dead; the Persian figure is a gross exaggeration. Modern scholars regard Greek losses as low (perhaps 1,000+) and Persian as heavy but unquantifiable.

description: The decisive land battle of the second Persian invasion of Greece, in which a Greek coalition under the Spartan Pausanias destroyed the Persian army of Mardonius in Boeotia. Coupled with the naval victory at Mycale, it ended the Persian threat to mainland Greece.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Plataea
Britannica: Battle of Plataea

name: Battle of Mycale
locations: Slopes of Mount Mycale, Ionia (near Samos, western Anatolia)

casualtyRange.notes: Ancient figures unreliable / no reliable estimate.

description: Fought on the Ionian coast on (traditionally) the same day as Plataea, the Greek fleet and landing force destroyed the beached Persian fleet and army at Mycale. The victory triggered a renewed revolt of the Ionian Greek cities against Persia and shifted the Greco-Persian Wars onto the Greek offensive.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Mycale
Britannica: Battle of Mycale

name: Battle of Lake Trasimene
locations: Northern shore of Lake Trasimene, Umbria, Italy

casualtyRange.notes: Roman dead reported ~15,000 with another ~15,000 captured; Carthaginian losses light (~1,500-2,500). Ancient figures, broadly accepted as a major Roman disaster.

description: Hannibal ambushed and destroyed a Roman army under the consul Gaius Flaminius along the shore of Lake Trasimene, one of the largest ambushes in military history. The disaster led Rome to appoint Fabius Maximus dictator and adopt a strategy of delay.

Livius.org (Jona Lendering)

name: Battle of the Metaurus

casualtyRange.notes: Carthaginian dead reported ~10,000 (Polybius) up to far higher in Livy; Roman dead ~2,000-8,000. Ancient figures diverge.

description: Roman consuls Livius Salinator and Claudius Nero destroyed the Carthaginian army of Hasdrubal Barca, Hannibal's brother, before it could reinforce him in southern Italy. Hasdrubal was killed and the strategic balance of the Second Punic War shifted decisively to Rome.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of the Metaurus

name: Battle of Ilipa
locations: Ilipa, near modern Alcalá del Río, Hispania Baetica (Spain)

casualtyRange.notes: Ancient figures unreliable / no reliable estimate. Carthaginian army destroyed but precise totals uncertain.

description: Scipio Africanus outmaneuvered a larger Carthaginian army under Hasdrubal Gisco and Mago in southern Spain through a sophisticated double-envelopment. The victory effectively ended Carthaginian power in the Iberian Peninsula.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Ilipa
Livius.org (Jona Lendering)

name: Battle of Baecula
locations: Baecula, near modern Santo Tomé, Hispania (Spain)

casualtyRange.notes: Ancient figures unreliable / no reliable estimate.

description: Scipio Africanus defeated Hasdrubal Barca's Carthaginian army in southern Spain, though Hasdrubal escaped with part of his force to march on Italy. It was Scipio's first major victory in the Iberian campaign of the Second Punic War.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Baecula

casualtyRange.notes: Three full Roman legions (XVII, XVIII, XIX) plus auxiliaries were annihilated, roughly 15,000-20,000 men; ancient sources give no precise total. Germanic losses unknown.

description: An alliance of Germanic tribes under Arminius ambushed and destroyed three Roman legions under Publius Quinctilius Varus in the forests east of the Rhine. casualtyRange.notes: Tacitus reports ~400 Roman dead and as many as 80,000 Britons killed; the British figure is almost certainly grossly exaggerated. Site and totals uncertain.

description: The Roman governor Suetonius Paulinus crushed the much larger British army of Queen Boudica, ending the Iceni-led revolt against Roman rule in Britain. Despite being heavily outnumbered, Roman discipline in a confined battlefield proved decisive.

description: A coalition under the Roman general Aetius and the Visigothic king Theodoric I checked Attila the Hun's invasion of Gaul in a massive and bloody battle. Though indecisive in casualties, it halted the Hunnic advance into the western empire.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of the Catalaunian Plains
Britannica: Battle of the Catalaunian Plains

name: Battle of Edessa

casualtyRange.notes: Ancient figures unreliable / no reliable estimate. Notable for the capture of an emperor rather than a casualty count.

description: Shapur I of the Sasanian Empire defeated and captured the Roman emperor Valerian near Edessa, an unprecedented humiliation for Rome. Valerian died in Persian captivity, and the event is commemorated in monumental Sasanian rock reliefs.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Edessa

name: Battle of Jingxing
locations: Jingxing Pass, Zhao territory (modern Hebei, China)
countries: Han (Liu Bang) forces under Han Xin

casualtyRange.notes: Ancient figures unreliable / no reliable estimate.

description: The Han general Han Xin defeated the much larger Zhao army by deploying his troops with their backs to a river, leaving them no retreat, the famous 'fighting with one's back to the river' stratagem. The victory was a key step in Liu Bang's conquest of northern China during the Chu-Han Contention.

name: Battle of Corupedium

casualtyRange.notes: Ancient figures unreliable / no reliable estimate.

description: The last battle between the original successors of Alexander the Great, in which Seleucus I Nicator defeated and killed Lysimachus in Lydia. The victory briefly left Seleucus master of most of Alexander's empire before his own assassination months later.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Corupedium
Livius.org (Jona Lendering)

name: Battle of Mount Gindarus

casualtyRange.notes: Ancient figures unreliable / no reliable estimate.

description: The Roman general Publius Ventidius Bassus defeated and killed the Parthian prince Pacorus I at Mount Gindarus in Syria, avenging the earlier Roman disaster at Carrhae. The victory drove the Parthians back across the Euphrates and stabilized Rome's eastern frontier.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Mount Gindarus
Cassius Dio, Roman History

name: Duar War
description: The Duar War (Anglo-Bhutanese War) of 1864-65 was a brief conflict in which British India defeated Bhutan despite some Bhutanese battlefield successes. The 1865 Treaty of Sinchula forced Bhutan to cede the Assam and Bengal Duars in exchange for an annual subsidy.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Duar War
Jaques, Dictionary of Battles and Sieges

name: Revolution of Ayutla
description: A liberal revolt proclaimed under the Plan of Ayutla in 1854 that aimed to oust the dictatorship of Antonio Lopez de Santa Anna. Its success in 1855 forced Santa Anna into exile and inaugurated the era of the Liberal Reform (La Reforma) in Mexico.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Revolution of Ayutla
Encyclopedia.com: Plan of Ayutla

name: War of the Supremes
description: A nationwide civil war in New Granada (modern Colombia), 1839-1842, sparked by a religious uprising in Pasto and the ambitions of regional caudillos calling themselves jefes supremos against President Jose Ignacio de Marquez. It was one of the first major civil wars of independent Colombia.

sources.label: Wikipedia: War of the Supremes
Encyclopedia.com: War of the Supremes

name: Anglo-Persian War
description: A war fought 1856-57 between Britain and Qajar Persia over Persian designs on Herat in Afghanistan. British and British-Indian forces captured Bushire and Mohammerah, and the Treaty of Paris (1857) forced Persia to withdraw from Herat.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Anglo-Persian War
Encyclopaedia Iranica: Anglo-Persian War (1856-57)

name: Bombardment of Kagoshima
description: Also called the Anglo-Satsuma War, this 15-17 August 1863 naval bombardment by a British squadron of Kagoshima sought compensation from the Satsuma Domain for the 1862 Namamugi Incident. The British lost 11 killed and Satsuma 5, and much of the city burned, but the clash paradoxically led to close British-Satsuma cooperation.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Bombardment of Kagoshima
Namamugi Incident (Wikipedia)

name: Franco-Trarzan War of 1825
description: A conflict between France and the Emirate of Trarza in the lower Senegal River region, arising from disputes over the gum-arabic trade and French expansion from Saint-Louis. It was an early episode in the French conquest of Senegal.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Franco-Trarzan War of 1825
French conquest of Senegal (Wikipedia)

name: Ecuadorian-Colombian War of 1863
description: A war (1862-63) between Gabriel Garcia Moreno's Ecuador and Tomas Cipriano de Mosquera's Colombia. At the Battle of Cuaspud (6 December 1863) the Colombians decisively defeated the invading Ecuadorian army, ending Garcia Moreno's expansionist ambitions.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Ecuadorian-Colombian War
GlobalSecurity: Ecuador-Colombia War 1863

name: Ragamuffin War
description: The Ragamuffin War (Guerra dos Farrapos), 1835-1845, was a republican secessionist uprising in southern Brazil's Rio Grande do Sul, led by Bento Goncalves, that proclaimed the Riograndense Republic. The decade-long conflict ended with the Treaty of Ponche Verde reintegrating the province.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Ragamuffin War
Encyclopedia.com: Farroupilha Revolt

name: Tirah Campaign
description: An 1897-98 British Indian frontier expedition against the Afridi and Orakzai Pashtun tribes of Tirah, mounted after the tribes seized the Khyber Pass. A force of nearly 35,000 under Sir William Lockhart fought a difficult mountain campaign.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Tirah campaign
Hutchinson, The Campaign in Tirah 1897-1898

name: Anglo-Manipur War
description: An 1891 war between British India and the Kingdom of Manipur, triggered by a palace coup. After British officers were executed at Imphal in March, British columns occupied the capital in April 1891 and annexed Manipur as a princely state.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Anglo-Manipur War
Britannica / Imphal historical accounts

name: Sokehs Rebellion
description: An uprising of the Sokehs people against German colonial rule on Pohnpei in the Caroline Islands, 1910-11. The rebels killed the German district commissioner before German naval forces suppressed the revolt; 15 captured leaders were executed by firing squad.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Sokehs rebellion
Micronesian Seminar: Sokehs Rebellion

description: Fought 22 September 1866 during the War of the Triple Alliance, the Battle of Curupayty was a catastrophic frontal assault by Brazilian and Argentine forces on entrenched Paraguayan positions. The attackers suffered thousands of casualties against negligible Paraguayan losses, stalling the allied advance for nearly a year.

name: Siege of Tuyen Quang
countries: China (Yunnan Army and Black Flag Army)
description: A four-month siege (November 1884-March 1885) during the Sino-French War in which a French garrison of 619 men, including French Foreign Legion companies, held the post of Tuyen Quang against vastly larger Chinese Yunnan Army and Black Flag forces until relieved. It became a celebrated Legion epic.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Siege of Tuyen Quang
Sino-French War (Wikipedia)

name: Battle of Caseros

casualtyRange.notes: Roughly 2,000 total casualties, predominantly Rosista forces; allied dead ~400.

description: Fought 3 February 1852 near Buenos Aires, the Battle of Caseros saw Justo Jose de Urquiza's allied army (with Brazilian and Uruguayan support) defeat the forces of Juan Manuel de Rosas, ending Rosas's 17-year rule and his exile to England. It opened the way for Argentine constitutional reorganization.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Caseros
Britannica: Battle of Caseros

name: Battle of Pavon
description: Fought 17 September 1861 in Santa Fe Province, the Battle of Pavon pitted Bartolome Mitre's Buenos Aires army against Justo Jose de Urquiza's Confederation forces. sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Pavon
Britannica: Battle of Pavon

name: First Battle of Bud Dajo

casualtyRange.notes: Moro dead, including women and children; Gen. Wood's estimate ~600, other estimates up to ~1,000. American losses ~18-21 killed.

description: Also called the Moro Crater Massacre, this March 1906 US Army action against Moros sheltering in the crater of Bud Dajo near Jolo during the Moro Rebellion killed hundreds of Moros, including many women and children, against minimal American losses. It became a notorious atrocity in the Philippine-American War era.

sources.label: Wikipedia: First Battle of Bud Dajo

name: Battle of Camaron
description: Fought 30 April 1863 during the Second French intervention in Mexico, the Battle of Camaron was a last stand by 65 French Foreign Legionnaires under Captain Jean Danjou against roughly 2,000-3,000 Mexican troops near Camaron de Tejeda. The near-total destruction of the detachment became the Legion's most celebrated feat of arms.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Camaron
Britannica: Battle of Camaron

name: Siege of Tashkent
description: The 1865 Russian capture of Tashkent (9 May-17 June 1865) was a decisive episode in the Russian conquest of Central Asia, defeating the Khanate of Kokand. The Kokandi leader Alimqul was killed, and Russia annexed the city, opening the way to the conquest of Bukhara.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Siege of Tashkent

name: Battle of Geok Tepe

description: The main event of Russia's 1880-81 campaign to conquer the Teke Turkmen, the Battle of Geok Tepe (January 1881) ended with General Skobelev storming the fortress and a massacre of fleeing Turkmen. name: Barrios' War of Reunification

description: An 1885 war launched when Guatemalan President Justo Rufino Barrios proclaimed himself President of a reunified Central America and invaded El Salvador. Barrios was killed at the Battle of Chalchuapa (2 April 1885), ending the campaign and the reunification attempt.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Barrios' War of Reunification
Wikipedia: Battle of Chalchuapa
