Battlefields Trust

name: Battle of Naseby

casualtyRange.notes: Royalist ~1,000 killed and ~5,000 captured; Parliamentarian losses ~400. Killed figure ~1,000-1,500, total Royalist casualties ~6,000.

description: On 14 June 1645 the Parliamentarian New Model Army under Fairfax and Cromwell destroyed the main Royalist field army of Charles I and Prince Rupert near Naseby, ending realistic Royalist hopes in the First English Civil War.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Naseby
Britannica: Battle of Naseby (1645)

name: Battle of Nagashino

casualtyRange.notes: Takeda dead variously estimated from ~3,000 up to ~10,000 (latter likely exaggerated); Oda-Tokugawa losses comparatively light.

description: Fought 28 June 1575 at Shitaragahara near Nagashino Castle, the allied forces of Oda Nobunaga and Tokugawa Ieyasu used massed arquebus volleys behind palisades to annihilate the Takeda cavalry under Katsuyori, a landmark in the use of firearms in Japan.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Nagashino
Stephen Turnbull, The Samurai Sourcebook

name: Battle of Sekigahara

casualtyRange.notes: Western Army losses commonly cited ~8,000 killed; some accounts give far higher totals (up to ~30,000+) including the rout. Highly uncertain.

description: On 21 October 1600 Tokugawa Ieyasu's Eastern Army defeated the Western Army loyal to Ishida Mitsunari at Sekigahara, the decisive battle that opened the way to the Tokugawa shogunate and over two centuries of unified rule.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Sekigahara
Stephen Turnbull, Sekigahara 1600

name: Battle of Khanwa
description: On 16 March 1527 Babur's Mughal army defeated the Rajput confederacy under Rana Sanga of Mewar near Khanwa (west of Agra), using gunpowder and field fortifications to consolidate Mughal power in northern India after Panipat.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Khanwa
John F. Richards, The Mughal Empire

name: Battle of Haldighati
description: On 18 June 1576 a Mughal army under Man Singh I fought the Mewar forces of Maharana Pratap at the Haldighati pass. The Mughals held the field, but Pratap escaped to continue a prolonged guerrilla resistance.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Haldighati
John F. Richards, The Mughal Empire

name: Battle of Sinhagad

casualtyRange.notes: ~300 Mughal and ~50 Maratha killed; Maratha commander Tanaji Malusare slain. Small-scale night assault.

description: On the night of 4 February 1670 Maratha forces under Tanaji Malusare scaled the cliffs to storm the Mughal-held Sinhagad (Kondhana) fort near Pune for Shivaji. The fort was taken but Tanaji was killed, an event celebrated in Maratha tradition.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Sinhagad
Stewart Gordon, The Marathas 1600-1818

name: Battle of Poltava

casualtyRange.notes: Swedish ~6,900-9,200 killed/wounded plus ~2,800 captured; Russian ~1,300 killed and ~3,300 wounded. Combined casualties commonly ~8,000-12,000.

description: On 8 July 1709 Tsar Peter I's Russian army decisively defeated the invading Swedish army of Charles XII near Poltava, the turning point of the Great Northern War that ended Sweden's status as a great power and began Russian ascendancy.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Poltava
Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts (4th ed., 2017)

name: Battle of Narva (1700)

casualtyRange.notes: Russian losses heavy: ~9,000-18,000 killed, wounded or captured; Swedish ~600-2,000. Estimates vary.

description: On 30 November 1700 a small Swedish army under Charles XII routed a much larger Russian force besieging Narva during a snowstorm, an early, spectacular Swedish victory in the Great Northern War.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Narva (1700)
Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts (4th ed., 2017)

name: Battle of Blenheim

casualtyRange.notes: Franco-Bavarian ~20,000+ casualties plus ~14,000 captured; Allied ~12,000 killed/wounded. Combined ~30,000-38,000.

description: On 13 August 1704 the Grand Alliance army under the Duke of Marlborough and Prince Eugene crushed a Franco-Bavarian army on the Danube near Blenheim, saving Vienna and breaking the myth of French invincibility in the War of the Spanish Succession.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Blenheim
Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts (4th ed., 2017)

name: Battle of Ramillies

casualtyRange.notes: French ~12,000-13,000 casualties (incl. many captured); Allied ~3,600. Combined ~15,000-16,000.

description: On 23 May 1706 Marlborough's Allied army decisively defeated the French under Villeroy at Ramillies in the Spanish Netherlands, leading to the rapid Allied conquest of much of the Spanish Netherlands.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Ramillies
Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts (4th ed., 2017)

name: Battle of Oudenarde

casualtyRange.notes: French ~6,000-8,000 casualties plus ~9,000 captured; Allied ~3,000. Combined battlefield casualties commonly ~9,000-15,000.

description: On 11 July 1708 the Allied army under Marlborough and Eugene defeated the French near Oudenarde on the Scheldt in a confused encounter battle, opening the road to the invasion of France.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Oudenarde
Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts (4th ed., 2017)

name: Battle of Malplaquet

casualtyRange.notes: Allied ~21,000-25,000 killed/wounded; French ~11,000-12,000. Combined ~32,000-36,000; bloodiest battle of the 18th century.

description: On 11 September 1709 the Allied army of Marlborough and Eugene won a narrow, extremely costly victory over the French under Villars near Malplaquet, the bloodiest battle of the 18th century, whose losses sapped Allied will to continue the war.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Malplaquet
Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts (4th ed., 2017)

name: Battle of Mollwitz

casualtyRange.notes: Prussian ~3,000 and Austrian ~4,000 killed or wounded. Combined ~7,000.

description: On 10 April 1741, the first battle of Frederick II of Prussia, the Prussian infantry secured victory over the Austrians at Mollwitz in Silesia during the First Silesian War, confirming Prussia's seizure of Silesia in the War of the Austrian Succession.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Mollwitz
Christopher Duffy, Frederick the Great: A Military Life

name: Battle of Fontenoy

casualtyRange.notes: French ~7,000-8,000 killed/wounded; Pragmatic Allies ~10,000-12,000 (incl. prisoners). Combined ~14,000-20,000.

description: On 11 May 1745, during the War of the Austrian Succession, the French army under Marshal Saxe defeated the Pragmatic Army of British, Dutch, Hanoverian and Austrian troops under the Duke of Cumberland near Tournai, leading to the French conquest of the Austrian Netherlands.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Fontenoy
Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts (4th ed., 2017)

name: Battle of Keresztes

casualtyRange.notes: Christian losses heavy after a near-victory collapsed into rout; combined dead frequently estimated 20,000-30,000. Figures uncertain.

description: Fought 24-26 October 1596 near Mezokeresztes, the Ottoman army of Mehmed III narrowly defeated a Habsburg-Transylvanian force during the Long Turkish War after the Christian army broke ranks to loot the Ottoman camp.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Keresztes
Caroline Finkel, Osman's Dream: The History of the Ottoman Empire

name: Battle of Jankau

casualtyRange.notes: Imperial army largely destroyed: ~4,000 killed and ~4,500 captured; Swedish losses lighter. Combined casualties ~6,000-10,000.

description: On 6 March 1645 the Swedish army under Lennart Torstensson annihilated an Imperial-Bavarian army under Hatzfeldt at Jankau in Bohemia, one of the most decisive Swedish victories of the late Thirty Years' War, opening the way toward Vienna.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Jankau
Peter H. Wilson, Europe's Tragedy

name: Battle of the Dunes (1658)

casualtyRange.notes: Spanish ~4,000 casualties (many captured); Franco-English ~400-1,000. Combined ~4,000-6,000.

description: On 14 June 1658, near Dunkirk, a French army under Turenne, reinforced by Cromwellian English New Model Army troops, defeated a Spanish army (which included exiled English Royalists) in the Franco-Spanish War, leading to the surrender of Dunkirk.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of the Dunes (1658)
Clodfelter, Warfare and Armed Conflicts (4th ed., 2017)

name: Battle of Wittstock

casualtyRange.notes: Total casualties ~7,000-10,000, predominantly among the Imperial-Saxon army.

description: On 4 October 1636 a Swedish army under Johan Baner and Alexander Leslie won a decisive victory over a larger Imperial-Saxon army south of Wittstock in Brandenburg, restoring Swedish prestige and prolonging Protestant resistance in the Thirty Years' War.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Wittstock
Britannica: Battle of Wittstock

name: Battle of Muye
description: Decisive battle in which King Wu of Zhou overthrew the Shang dynasty, capturing the capital and founding the Zhou dynasty. The victory became the classic justification for the Mandate of Heaven doctrine.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Muye
Xia–Shang–Zhou Chronology Project (date c. 1046 BC)

name: Battle of Kunyang
description: In 23 AD the future Emperor Guangwu, with a small Lulin rebel force, routed the vastly larger Xin army of Wang Mang at Kunyang, precipitating the collapse of the Xin dynasty and the restoration of the Han.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Kunyang
Hou Hanshu / Book of the Later Han

name: Goguryeo–Wei War
description: Series of invasions of Goguryeo by Cao Wei general Guanqiu Jian in 244–245, retaliating for a Goguryeo raid. The Wei sacked the capital Hwando and broke Goguryeo's tributary network, though the kingdom recovered.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Goguryeo–Wei War
Samguk Sagi; Sanguozhi

name: Goguryeo–Yan Wars
description: Conflict between Goguryeo and the Xianbei-led Former Yan; in 342 Murong Huang sacked Hwando, captured the queen mother and tens of thousands of Goguryeo people, and forced Goguryeo into submission.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Goguryeo–Yan Wars
Samguk Sagi; Book of Jin

name: Tang campaign against the Eastern Turks
description: Winter 629–630 offensive led by Tang general Li Jing that destroyed the Eastern Turkic Khaganate and captured Illig Qaghan, making Emperor Taizong the recognized 'Heavenly Khan' of the steppe.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Tang campaign against the Eastern Turks
Zizhi Tongjian; Old Book of Tang

name: Battle of Hulao
description: On 28 May 621 the Tang prince Li Shimin, with a smaller force entrenched at Hulao Pass, defeated and captured Dou Jiande of Xia, forcing the surrender of Wang Shichong and securing Tang control over north China.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Hulao
Zizhi Tongjian

name: Conquest of the Western Turks
description: Tang campaign of 655–657 led by general Su Dingfang that defeated Ashina Helu at the Battle of Irtysh River, destroyed the Western Turkic Khaganate, and extended Tang control over the Western Regions.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Conquest of the Western Turks
Old Book of Tang; Zizhi Tongjian

name: Tibetan capture of Chang'an
description: In November 763, exploiting Tang weakness after the An Lushan Rebellion, a large Tibetan army captured the Tang capital Chang'an for about fifteen days, briefly installing a puppet emperor before withdrawing with plunder.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Tang–Tibet relations
EBSCO Research Starters: Tibetans Capture Chang'an

name: Battle of Gwiju
description: Climactic 1019 battle of the Third Goryeo–Khitan War in which the Goryeo general Gang Gam-chan annihilated the retreating Khitan invasion army, after which the Liao never again invaded Korea.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Gwiju
Goryeosa (History of Goryeo)

name: Jingkang incident
description: Jurchen Jin siege and sack of the Northern Song capital Bianjing, culminating in January 1127 with the capture of Emperors Huizong and Qinzong and the imperial court, ending the Northern Song and forcing the relocation of the dynasty south.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Jingkang incident
Britannica: Jingkang Incident

name: Battle of Xiangyang
description: Protracted Mongol siege (1267–1273) of the twin Song fortress cities of Xiangyang and Fancheng, broken in 1273 with the aid of counterweight trebuchets, opening the Yangtze to the Yuan conquest of the Southern Song.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Xiangyang
De Re Militari: The Mongol Siege of Xiangyang and Fan-ch'eng

name: Battle of Cheoin
description: 1232 battle of the second Mongol invasion of Korea in which Goryeo defenders at Cheoin fortress held off the Mongols and the commander Saritai was killed by an arrow, prompting the Mongol withdrawal.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Cheoin
Goryeosa (History of Goryeo)

name: Sambyeolcho Rebellion
description: 1270–1273 revolt by the Sambyeolcho elite military corps against the pro-Mongol Goryeo court at the close of the Mongol invasions, resisting from island bases until crushed by combined Goryeo–Yuan forces on Jeju.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Sambyeolcho Rebellion
Goryeosa

name: Battle of Yamen

casualtyRange.notes: Traditional accounts report over 100,000 dead, including officials and women who drowned. This is a chronicle figure and likely imprecise.

description: Naval battle of 19 March 1279 marking the last stand of the Southern Song; the Yuan fleet destroyed the chained-together Song armada, and with the drowning of the boy-emperor Zhao Bing the Song dynasty was extinguished.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Yamen
Naval History Magazine (USNI), 'A Clash of Fleets, A Dynasty's End'

name: Heiji Rebellion
description: 1159–1160 power struggle in Kyoto between the Taira and Minamoto clans following their joint victory in the Hōgen Rebellion. Taira no Kiyomori's triumph established Taira dominance and set the stage for the Genpei War.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Heiji rebellion
Heiji Monogatari tradition

name: Battle of Okehazama
description: On 12 June 1560 Oda Nobunaga, heavily outnumbered, launched a surprise attack and killed Imagawa Yoshimoto, vaulting the Oda clan to the front rank of Sengoku warlords and launching Nobunaga's drive toward unification.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Okehazama
Shinchō Kōki (chronicle of Nobunaga)

name: Siege of Odawara
description: Toyotomi Hideyoshi's 1590 siege of the Hōjō stronghold at Odawara, conducted largely by blockade and intimidation with some 220,000 troops. The Hōjō surrender effectively completed the unification of Japan.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Siege of Odawara (1590)
EBSCO Research Starters: Odawara Campaign

name: Battle of Hansan Island
description: On 14 August 1592 Admiral Yi Sun-sin's Joseon fleet, using the 'crane wing' formation, destroyed or captured most of a large Japanese fleet near Hansan Island, halting Japanese naval operations during the Imjin War.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Hansan Island
Yi Sun-sin, Nanjung Ilgi (War Diary)

name: Battle of Chilcheollyang
description: Night battle of 28 August 1597 in which a Japanese fleet destroyed nearly the entire Joseon navy under Won Gyun, who had replaced the disgraced Yi Sun-sin. It was Korea's only major naval defeat of the war.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Chilcheollyang
Annals of the Joseon Dynasty

name: Battle of Sarhū

casualtyRange.notes: Ming accounts claim 45,000–60,000 dead across four armies; modern quantitative analyses suggest 10,000–20,000 is more realistic.

description: Series of 1619 battles in which Nurhaci's Later Jin cavalry annihilated the four converging Ming armies (with a Joseon contingent), a decisive turning point in the Manchu rise that led to the Qing conquest of China.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Sarhū
Kenneth Swope, The Military Collapse of China's Ming Dynasty

name: Later Jin invasion of Joseon
description: 1627 invasion led by the Later Jin prince Amin with roughly 30,000 troops, which overran northern Korea and forced Joseon into a tributary 'brotherhood' agreement with the Manchus while it still leaned toward Ming China.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Later Jin invasion of Joseon
Annals of the Joseon Dynasty

name: Qing invasion of Joseon
description: Winter 1636–1637 invasion by the newly proclaimed Qing under Hong Taiji, which besieged King Injo at Namhansanseong and forced Joseon to submit as a Qing tributary and sever its ties to the Ming.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Qing invasion of Joseon
Annals of the Joseon Dynasty

name: Jingnan campaign
description: Three-year Ming civil war (1399–1402) in which Zhu Di, Prince of Yan, overthrew his nephew the Jianwen Emperor, captured Nanjing, and took the throne as the Yongle Emperor.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Jingnan campaign
Ming Shi (History of Ming)

name: Jiajing wokou raids
description: Peak of mid-16th-century 'wokou' pirate raiding (mostly Chinese, with Japanese and Portuguese crews) along China's southeast coast during the Jiajing reign, driven by Ming maritime-prohibition policy and suppressed by generals such as Qi Jiguang by 1567.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Jiajing wokou raids
Ming Shi; Kwan-wai So, Japanese Piracy in Ming China

name: Khoshut conquest of Tibet
description: Campaigns of 1639–1642 in which the Oirat Mongol leader Güshi Khan defeated the Beri king and the Tsangpa ruler, took Shigatse, and brought all Tibet under Gelug control, founding the Khoshut Khanate and installing the 5th Dalai Lama's Ganden Phodrang government.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Khoshut Khanate
Wikipedia: Güshi Khan

name: Battle of Jao Modo
description: On 12 June 1696 a Qing army personally led by the Kangxi Emperor defeated Galdan Boshugtu Khan's Dzungar-Mongol force, securing Khalkha Mongolia for the Qing and breaking Galdan, who died the following year.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Jao Modo
Peter Perdue, China Marches West

name: Liaoshen campaign

casualtyRange.notes: Nationalist forces suffered over 470,000 casualties (killed, wounded, captured); PLA losses about 69,000. Combined ~539,000.

description: First of the three decisive campaigns of the Chinese Civil War (September–November 1948), in which Lin Biao's Communist Northeast Field Army destroyed the Nationalist armies in Manchuria, capturing Jinzhou, Changchun, and Shenyang.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Liaoshen campaign
Odd Arne Westad, Decisive Encounters

name: Battle of Lechfeld (955)
description: Over 10-12 August 955, King Otto I of Germany decisively defeated a large Magyar raiding army on the Lechfeld floodplain south of Augsburg. The victory effectively ended major Hungarian incursions into Western Europe and bolstered Otto's claim to imperial authority.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Lechfeld
Britannica: Battle of Lechfeld

name: Battle of Tinchebray
description: On 28 September 1106, King Henry I of England defeated and captured his elder brother Robert Curthose, Duke of Normandy, at Tinchebray in southwest Normandy. The victory reunited England and Normandy under Henry's rule.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Tinchebray
English Monarchs: Battle of Tinchebray

name: Battle of Brémule
description: On 20 August 1119, Henry I of England defeated Louis VI of France at Brémule in the Norman Vexin, repelling a French invasion of Normandy. Despite some 900 knights engaged, chroniclers record only three killed and about 140 French knights captured.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Brémule
De Re Militari (Orderic Vitalis on Brémule)

name: Battle of Legnano
description: On 29 May 1176, the Lombard League defeated Emperor Frederick Barbarossa near Legnano northwest of Milan, ending his fifth and last attempt to subdue the northern Italian communes by force. The defeat pushed Frederick toward a diplomatic settlement embodied in the 1183 Peace of Constance.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Legnano
EBSCO Research Starters: Battle of Legnano

name: Battle of Cortenuova
description: On 27 November 1237, Holy Roman Emperor Frederick II defeated the Second Lombard League at Cortenuova in the territory of Bergamo, a major victory in the renewed Guelph-Ghibelline conflict in northern Italy.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Cortenuova
Britannica: Battle of Cortenuova

name: Battle of Worringen

casualtyRange.notes: Estimated ~1,100 dead on the Guelders/Cologne side and ~40 on the Brabant side; figures are chronicle-derived approximations.

description: On 5 June 1288, Duke John I of Brabant decisively defeated the Archbishop of Cologne and the Count of Luxembourg near Worringen, the climactic battle of the War of the Limburg Succession. The victory added Limburg to Brabant and weakened the archbishop's temporal power over Cologne.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Worringen
Oxford Reference: Battle of Worringen

name: Battle on the Marchfeld
description: On 26 August 1278, Rudolf I of Habsburg, allied with King Ladislaus IV of Hungary, defeated and killed King Ottokar II of Bohemia in one of the largest cavalry battles of medieval Central Europe. The outcome ended Přemyslid expansion and launched the rise of the House of Habsburg in Austria.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle on the Marchfeld
Deutschlandmuseum: Battle of Dürnkrut
HCED — Miller & Bakar (2023), Historical Conflict Event Dataset, J. Conflict Resolution 67(2-3)
Jaques, Dictionary of Battles and Sieges (HCED primary source)

name: Battle of Covadonga
description: Around 722, Pelagius of Asturias defeated an Umayyad force in the mountainous terrain at Covadonga in the Picos de Europa. Though small in scale, it secured a Christian foothold in northern Iberia and is traditionally regarded as the start of the Reconquista.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Covadonga
Britannica: Battle of Covadonga

name: Battle of Ourique
description: On 25 July 1139, the forces of Count Afonso Henriques defeated an Almoravid army in the region of Ourique in southern Portugal. The victory is traditionally linked to Afonso's proclamation as the first King of Portugal.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Ourique
Britannica: Battle of Ourique

name: Battle of Muret
countries: Crown of Aragon and County of Toulouse
description: On 12 September 1213, a small crusader force under Simon de Montfort defeated a much larger allied army under King Peter II of Aragon and Count Raymond VI of Toulouse near Muret. Peter II was killed; the outcome ended Aragonese influence in Languedoc and advanced French royal control during the Albigensian Crusade.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Muret
Britannica: Battle of Muret

name: Battle of Nájera
description: On 3 April 1367, an Anglo-Gascon and Castilian army led by Edward the Black Prince defeated the Franco-Castilian forces of Henry of Trastámara near Nájera in La Rioja, restoring Pedro of Castile to his throne during the First Castilian Civil War, a theatre of the Hundred Years' War.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Nájera
De Re Militari (Villalon & Kagay, eds., on Nájera)

name: Battle of Clontarf
description: On 23 April 1014, the High King Brian Boru's forces defeated a Norse-Irish alliance led by Sigtrygg Silkbeard of Dublin and Máel Mórda of Leinster at Clontarf near Dublin. Brian was killed in the aftermath, making it a costly, near-pyrrhic victory that ended the major Viking threat to Irish kingship.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Clontarf
Britannica: Battle of Clontarf

name: Battle of Stamford Bridge
description: On 25 September 1066, King Harold Godwinson of England destroyed an invading Norwegian army under King Harald Hardrada and Tostig Godwinson at Stamford Bridge in Yorkshire; both invading leaders were killed. The hard-won victory left Harold's army depleted just before the Norman invasion at Hastings.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Stamford Bridge
Britannica: Battle of Stamford Bridge

name: Battle of Edington
description: In May 878, King Alfred the Great of Wessex defeated the Danish Great Heathen Army under Guthrum near Edington in Wiltshire. The victory halted the Viking conquest of Wessex and led to Guthrum's baptism and the Treaty of Wedmore.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Edington
Britannica: Battle of Edington

name: Battle of Dorylaeum (1097)
description: On 1 July 1097, the army of the First Crusade defeated the Seljuk Turks under Kilij Arslan I near Dorylaeum in Anatolia after Bohemond's vanguard was nearly overwhelmed before relief arrived. The victory opened the crusaders' route across Asia Minor toward Antioch.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Dorylaeum (1097)
Britannica: Battle of Dorylaeum

name: Battle of Ascalon
description: On 12 August 1099, shortly after capturing Jerusalem, a crusader army under Godfrey of Bouillon routed a numerically superior Fatimid relief army under vizier al-Afdal near Ascalon. Often considered the final action of the First Crusade, it secured the newly established Kingdom of Jerusalem.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Ascalon
Foreign Exchanges: Battle of Ascalon (1099)

name: Battle of the Field of Blood
description: On 28 June 1119, the Artuqid ruler Ilghazi of Mardin annihilated the field army of the Principality of Antioch under Roger of Salerno near the pass of Sarmada in northern Syria. Roger was killed and the crusader force was nearly destroyed, severely weakening Antioch.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of the Field of Blood
The Medieval Review (Morton, The Field of Blood)

name: Siege of Edessa (1144)
description: From 28 November to 24 December 1144, the atabeg Imad al-Din Zengi besieged and captured Edessa, capital of the first crusader state. Its fall shocked Latin Christendom and became the immediate catalyst for the Second Crusade.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Siege of Edessa (1144)
Britannica: Siege of Edessa

name: Battle of Mansurah (1250)
description: From 8 to 11 February 1250, the Seventh Crusade under Louis IX of France clashed with Ayyubid forces at Mansurah in the Nile Delta. An initial crusader assault led by Robert of Artois was crushed; the failure, followed by disease and retreat, led to Louis IX's capture at Fariskur.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Mansurah (1250)
EBSCO Research Starters: Battle of Mansura

name: Battle of La Forbie
countries: Kingdom of Jerusalem and Ayyubid allies

casualtyRange.notes: Total dead across allied knights, sergeants and infantry estimated between ~5,000 and over 16,000; military orders nearly wiped out (e.g. of ~348 Templar knights only ~36 survived).

description: On 17-18 October 1244, an Egyptian Ayyubid army reinforced by Khwarezmian mercenaries crushed the combined armies of the Kingdom of Jerusalem and its Ayyubid Syrian allies near La Forbie northeast of Gaza. The catastrophic defeat shattered crusader military strength in the Holy Land and helped prompt the Seventh Crusade.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of La Forbie
Medievalists.net: The Battle of La Forbie (1244) and its Aftermath

name: Battle of Kleidion
description: On 29 July 1014, Byzantine Emperor Basil II destroyed the army of Tsar Samuel of Bulgaria in the Belasitsa mountain passes near Klyuch. Basil reportedly blinded thousands of captives, earning the epithet 'Bulgar-Slayer'; the defeat hastened the collapse of the First Bulgarian Empire.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Kleidion
Medievalists.net: Did Basil II blind 15,000 prisoners?

name: Battle of Civitate
description: On 18 June 1053, the Normans of Apulia under Humphrey of Hauteville defeated a Swabian-Italian-Lombard army organised by Pope Leo IX near Civitate; the pope was captured. The victory consolidated Norman power in southern Italy and forced the papacy toward accommodation with the Normans.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Civitate
World History Encyclopedia: Battle of Civitate

name: Battle of the Kalka River
locations: north of the Sea of Azov
description: On 31 May 1223, a Mongol reconnaissance army under Jebe and Subutai decisively defeated a coalition of Rus princes and Cumans on the Kalka River north of the Sea of Azov. The disaster was the first clash between the Rus and the Mongols, foreshadowing the full invasion of 1237-1240.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of the Kalka River
Britannica: Battle of the Kalka River (1223)

name: Battle of Legnica
description: On 9 April 1241, a Mongol army defeated combined Polish and Moravian forces under Duke Henry II the Pious of Silesia at Legnickie Pole; Henry was killed. Together with the victory at Mohi two days later, it demonstrated Mongol dominance over the chivalry of Central Europe.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Legnica
Britannica: Battle of Legnica (1241)

name: Battle of Mohi
description: On 11 April 1241, the Mongol army under Batu Khan and Subutai crushed the Hungarian army of King Béla IV at Mohi on the Sajó River. The defeat opened Hungary to devastating Mongol occupation until the Mongols withdrew in 1242.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Mohi
Britannica: Battle of Mohi

name: Battle of the Terek River
description: In mid-April 1395, Timur (Tamerlane) defeated Tokhtamysh of the Golden Horde on the Terek River in the North Caucasus, the decisive battle of the Tokhtamysh-Timur war. Timur then sacked Sarai, Astrakhan and Azov, crippling the Golden Horde's power.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of the Terek River
Foreign Exchanges: Battle of the Terek River (1395)

name: Battle of the Vorskla River
countries: Grand Duchy of Lithuania and allies
description: On 12 August 1399, the Golden Horde forces of Temür Qutlugh and Edigu decisively defeated Grand Duke Vytautas of Lithuania and his ally Tokhtamysh on the Vorskla River near Poltava. Many Lithuanian and Ruthenian princes were killed, checking Lithuanian expansion into the steppe.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of the Vorskla River
Britannica: Battle of the Vorskla River

name: First Battle of Tarain
description: On 14 January 1191, the Rajput confederacy under Prithviraj Chauhan defeated the invading Ghurid forces of Muhammad of Ghor at Tarain (Taraori) north of Delhi, wounding Muhammad and forcing his retreat. The reprieve proved temporary, as the Ghurids returned and won the second battle in 1192.

sources.label: Wikipedia: First Battle of Tarain
BYJU's IAS: First Battle of Tarain (1191)

name: Second Battle of Tarain
description: In 1192, the Ghurid forces of Muhammad of Ghor decisively defeated the Rajput confederacy of Prithviraj Chauhan at Tarain (Taraori). The victory broke Rajput power in the region and laid the foundation for Muslim rule in northern India and the later Delhi Sultanate.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Second Battle of Tarain
RajRAS: Battles of Tarain

name: Battle of Kili
description: In 1299, the Delhi Sultanate army of Alauddin Khalji confronted a large invading Mongol force of the Chagatai Khanate under Qutlugh Khwaja near Kili outside Delhi. Though Alauddin's general Zafar Khan was killed in an ambush, the Mongols withdrew, ending the threat to Delhi.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Kili
History of War: Battle of Kili, 1299

name: Battle of Dupplin Moor
description: On 11-12 August 1332, a small force backing the claimant Edward Balliol, using dismounted men-at-arms flanked by archers, crushed a much larger Scottish army under the regent Donald, Earl of Mar, southeast of Perth. The first major battle of the Second War of Scottish Independence pioneered tactics later used at Halidon Hill and Crécy.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Dupplin Moor
Britannica: Battle of Dupplin Moor

name: Battle of Halidon Hill
countries: Kingdom of England (Edward III and Edward Balliol)

casualtyRange.notes: Scottish chronicles claim ~10,000 killed; modern historians estimate Scottish dead nearer ~2,900. English losses were minimal (single-digit to low double-digit).

description: On 19 July 1333, an English army under Edward III defeated a Scottish army under Sir Archibald Douglas at Halidon Hill northwest of Berwick. English longbowmen positioned on the slopes inflicted heavy casualties as the Scots attacked uphill, a tactical template for later Hundred Years' War battles.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Halidon Hill
Britannica: Battle of Halidon Hill

name: Battle of Auray
description: On 29 September 1364, the Anglo-Breton army of John de Montfort, with English troops under John Chandos, defeated and killed Charles of Blois near Auray, ending the War of the Breton Succession. The 1365 Treaty of Guérande recognised the Montfort line as dukes of Brittany.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Auray
Britannica: War of the Breton Succession

name: Battle of Roosebeke
description: On 27 November 1382, the French royal army of Charles VI defeated the Flemish urban militia under Philip van Artevelde on the Goudberg near Westrozebeke; Artevelde was killed. The victory crushed the Ghent-led Flemish revolt and reasserted French and comital authority in Flanders.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Roosebeke
Encyclopedia.com: Roosebeke, battle of

name: Battle of Otterburn
description: In August 1388, a Scottish raiding force under James, Earl of Douglas, defeated an English army under Henry 'Hotspur' Percy in a night battle at Otterburn in Northumberland. Douglas was killed and Percy captured; the clash became celebrated in border ballad tradition.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Otterburn
Battlefields Trust: Battle of Otterburn

name: Battle of Aljubarrota
description: On 14 August 1385, the outnumbered Portuguese army of John I, commanded by Nuno Álvares Pereira and aided by English archers, decisively defeated the invading Castilian army of John I of Castile at São Jorge near Aljubarrota. The victory secured Portuguese independence and ended the 1383-85 succession crisis.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Aljubarrota
Britannica: Battle of Aljubarrota

name: Battle of Sempach
description: On 9 July 1386, the forces of the Old Swiss Confederacy defeated a Habsburg army near Sempach in Lucerne; Duke Leopold III of Austria and many Austrian nobles were killed. The victory was a turning point in consolidating Swiss independence from Habsburg overlordship.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Sempach
Britannica: Battle of Sempach

name: Battle of Tagliacozzo
description: On 23 August 1268, Charles of Anjou defeated the Ghibelline army of the young Hohenstaufen claimant Conradin on the Palentine plains near Tagliacozzo. Conradin's subsequent capture and execution ended Hohenstaufen power in Italy and secured Angevin rule over Sicily and the south.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Tagliacozzo
Britannica: Battle of Tagliacozzo

name: Battle of Visby

casualtyRange.notes: An estimated ~1,800 Gotland yeomen and peasants died; ~2,000 bodies were later disinterred from mass graves at Korsbetningen. Danish losses unknown.

description: On 27 July 1361, the invading army of King Valdemar IV of Denmark defeated a poorly equipped Gotland peasant militia outside the walls of Visby. The mass graves later excavated at Korsbetningen, with armoured skeletons, make it one of the best-documented medieval battlefields archaeologically.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Visby
Historiska museet: Medieval Massacre (Visby)

name: Battle of Lewes
description: On 14 May 1264, the baronial army of Simon de Montfort defeated King Henry III on the downs above Lewes in Sussex, a key battle of the Second Barons' War. The royalist defeat forced the Mise of Lewes, making de Montfort the effective ruler of England.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Lewes
Historic England Battlefield Report: Lewes 1264

name: Paraguayan Civil War (1947)

casualtyRange.notes: Estimates vary widely (commonly 20,000–30,000); chaotic records and mass displacement make figures uncertain.

description: A 1947 civil war in Paraguay pitting Higinio Morínigo's Colorado-backed government against a Febrerista-Liberal-Communist alliance, with 'barefoot' (pynandí) peasant militias suffering heavy losses. Government victory paved the way for Colorado dominance and Stroessner's later dictatorship.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Paraguayan Civil War (1947)
UCDP Conflict Encyclopedia

name: Dhofar Rebellion

casualtyRange.notes: Approx. 8,000 noncombatant deaths estimated; 719 Iranian troops killed; precise totals never compiled.

description: A 1965–1976 leftist insurgency in Oman's Dhofar region against the Al Bu Said sultanate and British presence, backed by South Yemen and waged by the Dhofar Liberation Front and later the Marxist PFLOAG. British, Iranian and Jordanian support helped the sultanate defeat it by 1976.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Dhofar rebellion
UCDP Conflict Encyclopedia

name: 1958 Lebanon crisis

casualtyRange.notes: Estimates of fighting deaths vary; roughly 1,300–4,000 over the months of unrest.

description: A 1958 political-religious crisis in Lebanon between President Camille Chamoun's government and a largely Muslim, pan-Arabist opposition, prompting US military intervention (Operation Blue Bat). It ended with Chamoun's term completed and Fuad Chehab elected president.

sources.label: Wikipedia: 1958 Lebanon crisis
UCDP Conflict Encyclopedia

name: Revolución Libertadora (1955)

casualtyRange.notes: Over 300 killed in the June 1955 Plaza de Mayo bombing alone; total coup-related deaths uncertain.

description: The September 1955 civic-military coup that overthrew Argentine President Juan Perón, preceded by the June 1955 bombing of Plaza de Mayo that killed over 300 civilians. It installed a military dictatorship and banned Peronism for years.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Revolución Libertadora
UCDP Conflict Encyclopedia

name: Annexation of Goa

casualtyRange.notes: 22 Indians and 30 Portuguese killed in the ~36-hour operation.

description: India's December 1961 military action (Operation Vijay) that annexed the Portuguese territories of Goa, Daman and Diu, ending 451 years of Portuguese rule in India after a roughly 36-hour campaign.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Annexation of Goa
UCDP Conflict Encyclopedia

name: Caracazo

casualtyRange.notes: Official toll 276; human-rights estimates run as high as ~3,000.

description: A wave of riots, looting and state repression beginning 27 February 1989 around Caracas after President Carlos Andrés Pérez imposed IMF-backed austerity. Security forces' lethal crackdown left hundreds to thousands dead and helped catalyze later Venezuelan upheaval.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Caracazo
UCDP Conflict Encyclopedia

name: Telangana Rebellion

casualtyRange.notes: Commonly cited ~4,000 peasant deaths, but figures are contested and vary from several hundred to tens of thousands; treated as an uncertain range rather than a flat fact.

description: A communist-led peasant insurrection of 1946–1951 in the Telangana region against landlords and the princely state of Hyderabad, demanding land reform. It was suppressed after India's annexation of Hyderabad, and the Communist Party formally ended it in October 1951.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Telangana Rebellion
UCDP Conflict Encyclopedia

name: Annexation of Hyderabad

casualtyRange.notes: Sunderlal Committee: 30,000–40,000 dead; some observers estimated 200,000+, largely communal massacres.

description: India's September 1948 military operation (Operation Polo) that annexed the princely state of Hyderabad, ending its bid for independence. The brief campaign was followed by large-scale communal massacres, mostly of Muslims, with death estimates ranging from tens of thousands to over 200,000.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Annexation of Hyderabad
UCDP Conflict Encyclopedia

name: Naxalbari uprising

casualtyRange.notes: Small initial death toll; the uprising's significance is as the trigger of the broader Naxalite movement.

description: An armed peasant revolt in 1967 in the Naxalbari area of West Bengal in which peasants seized land from landlords, sparking the broader Naxalite-Maoist insurgency in India. The localized revolt was quickly suppressed but became a lasting political movement.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Naxalbari uprising
UCDP Conflict Encyclopedia

name: Bizerte crisis

casualtyRange.notes: Approximately 630 Tunisians and 24 French killed in three days of fighting.

description: A July 1961 clash after Tunisia blockaded the French naval base at Bizerte to force its evacuation. A three-day battle left some 630 Tunisians and 24 French dead before France reasserted control; it withdrew fully in 1963.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Bizerte crisis
UCDP Conflict Encyclopedia

name: Costa Rican Civil War

casualtyRange.notes: About 2,000 deaths commonly cited; some sources give up to 4,000 in the 44-day war.

description: A 44-day civil war in 1948 sparked by the annulment of a contested presidential election, in which José Figueres's National Liberation Army defeated government and allied communist forces. It led to the abolition of Costa Rica's army and a lasting democratic order.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Costa Rican Civil War
UCDP Conflict Encyclopedia

name: 1982 Hama massacre

casualtyRange.notes: Estimates range from 5,000 to 40,000 killed, including about 1,000 soldiers.

description: A 27-day siege and assault on the Syrian city of Hama in February 1982 by Hafez al-Assad's army and Defense Companies to crush a Muslim Brotherhood uprising. Casualty estimates range from 5,000 to 40,000, making it one of the deadliest single acts of state violence in modern Middle Eastern history.

sources.label: Wikipedia: 1982 Hama massacre
UCDP Conflict Encyclopedia

name: Anfal campaign

casualtyRange.notes: Human Rights Watch estimated 50,000–100,000 deaths; Kurdish sources cite up to 182,000.

description: A genocidal counterinsurgency campaign waged by Saddam Hussein's government against Iraqi Kurds in 1986–1989, involving chemical attacks, mass executions, deportations and the destruction of thousands of villages. Human Rights Watch estimated 50,000–100,000 killed; it is internationally recognized as genocide.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Anfal campaign
UCDP Conflict Encyclopedia

name: Halabja massacre

casualtyRange.notes: About 5,000 killed and over 10,000 injured in the chemical attack of 16 March 1988.

description: A large-scale chemical weapons attack by Iraqi forces on the Kurdish town of Halabja on 16 March 1988, during the Anfal campaign, killing roughly 5,000 civilians and injuring over 10,000. It is the largest chemical attack against a civilian population in history.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Halabja massacre
UCDP Conflict Encyclopedia

name: 1959 Tibetan uprising

casualtyRange.notes: PRIO estimates ~10,000 Tibetan and 2,000 PLA battle deaths; Tibetan sources cite far higher tolls.

description: An armed uprising in Lhasa in March 1959 against Chinese rule, which was crushed by the People's Liberation Army and led the 14th Dalai Lama to flee into exile in India. Casualty estimates range from around 10,000 battle deaths to far higher tolls cited by Tibetan sources.

sources.label: Wikipedia: 1959 Tibetan uprising
UCDP Conflict Encyclopedia

name: Cyprus Emergency

casualtyRange.notes: About 371 British military and 21 police killed plus Cypriot fighters and civilians; total roughly 500+.

description: An anti-colonial insurgency in British Cyprus from 1955 to 1959 waged by EOKA, a Greek Cypriot guerrilla organisation seeking union (enosis) with Greece. It ended with the 1959 Zürich-London agreements granting Cyprus independence in 1960.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Cyprus Emergency
UCDP Conflict Encyclopedia

name: 1991 Iraqi uprisings

casualtyRange.notes: Estimates of those killed in suppression range widely from tens of thousands to ~180,000+, plus mass displacement.

description: Mass Shia and Kurdish uprisings (the Sha'aban Intifada) against Saddam Hussein in March–April 1991 following the Gulf War ceasefire, which briefly seized most Iraqi provinces before being brutally crushed. Estimates of those killed in the suppression range from tens of thousands to well over 100,000.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Sha'aban Intifada
UCDP Conflict Encyclopedia

name: 2011 Bahraini uprising

casualtyRange.notes: BICI found 35 deaths to mid-April 2011; cumulative toll reached ~122 by 2013.

description: An Arab Spring pro-democracy uprising in Bahrain beginning February 2011, centered on Manama's Pearl Roundabout and led mainly by the Shia majority. It was suppressed with the help of Saudi-led GCC forces; cumulative deaths reached over 120 in the following years.

sources.label: Wikipedia: 2011 Bahraini uprising
UCDP Conflict Encyclopedia

name: Jeju uprising

casualtyRange.notes: Official commission identified 14,373 victims; total death toll estimated up to 30,000.

description: An insurrection and brutal counterinsurgency on South Korea's Jeju Island from April 1948 to May 1949, in which leftist rebels rose against the US-backed government and elections. Security forces caused the overwhelming majority of an estimated 14,000–30,000 deaths.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Jeju uprising
UCDP Conflict Encyclopedia

name: Insurgency in Balochistan

casualtyRange.notes: Ongoing; thousands of combatants and civilians killed and many enforced disappearances; point-in-time estimate.

description: An ongoing low-level separatist insurgency in Pakistan's Balochistan province (with spillover into Iran), driven by grievances over political marginalisation, resource control and enforced disappearances. The latest phase intensified from 2004 and continues, with thousands of deaths (figures are a point-in-time snapshot, ongoing).

sources.label: Wikipedia: Insurgency in Balochistan
UCDP Conflict Encyclopedia

name: Operation Blue Star

casualtyRange.notes: Official toll 410 killed; Sikh groups dispute and cite figures in the thousands.

description: An Indian Army operation from 1 to 10 June 1984 to remove Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale and armed militants from the Golden Temple complex in Amritsar. The assault on Sikhism's holiest site caused official casualties of 410 (disputed as far higher) and led to Indira Gandhi's assassination later that year.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Operation Blue Star
UCDP Conflict Encyclopedia

name: Tuareg rebellion (1990–1995)

casualtyRange.notes: At least ~300 killed (including the Tchin-Tabaradene massacre); totals uncertain.

description: A Tuareg insurgency across northern Mali and Niger from 1990 to 1995 seeking autonomy after famine, displacement and political repression. It featured army reprisals such as the Tchin-Tabaradene massacre and ended in negotiated peace settlements.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Tuareg rebellion (1990–1995)
UCDP Conflict Encyclopedia

name: 1979 Herat uprising

casualtyRange.notes: Aerial bombardment and recapture left an estimated 3,000–25,000 dead.

description: A March 1979 uprising and army mutiny in Herat against Afghanistan's communist government, during which Soviet advisers were among those killed. The regime retook the city after aerial bombardment, leaving an estimated 3,000 to 25,000 dead and accelerating the slide toward Soviet intervention.

sources.label: Wikipedia: 1979 Herat uprising
UCDP Conflict Encyclopedia

name: Aden Emergency

casualtyRange.notes: About 90–92 British military and 17 British civilians killed; total deaths roughly 2,000 including Yemenis.

description: An anti-colonial insurgency from 1963 to 1967 in Aden and the Federation of South Arabia, waged by the NLF and FLOSY against British rule. It culminated in Britain's withdrawal and the establishment of independent South Yemen.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Aden Emergency
UCDP Conflict Encyclopedia

name: 1953 Iranian coup d'état

casualtyRange.notes: About 300 killed in Tehran fighting, plus executions and deaths in custody afterward.

description: A CIA- and MI6-orchestrated coup in August 1953 (Operation Ajax) that overthrew Iran's democratically elected prime minister Mohammad Mosaddegh and restored the Shah's power. Roughly 300 died in Tehran's street fighting; the coup reshaped Iranian politics for decades.

sources.label: Wikipedia: 1953 Iranian coup d'état
UCDP Conflict Encyclopedia

name: Buddhist Uprising (1966)
countries: Buddhist movement and dissident ARVN units

casualtyRange.notes: Several hundred killed in clashes between government forces and the Struggle Movement; precise total uncertain.

description: A 1966 revolt by Buddhist activists and dissident army units (the Struggle Movement) in central South Vietnam against the military government of Nguyễn Cao Kỳ. Government forces crushed the movement in Da Nang and Huế after weeks of fighting.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Buddhist Uprising
UCDP Conflict Encyclopedia

name: Black September (Jordan)

casualtyRange.notes: Estimates range from ~1,500–2,000 to 7,000–8,000 killed.

description: A 1970–1971 conflict in which the Jordanian army under King Hussein expelled Palestinian fedayeen organisations that had become a state-within-a-state. The fighting, concentrated in Amman, killed thousands and forced the PLO to relocate to Lebanon.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Black September
UCDP Conflict Encyclopedia

name: Chittagong Hill Tracts conflict
countries: Parbatya Chattagram Jana Samhati Samiti / Shanti Bahini

casualtyRange.notes: Around 30,000 commonly cited as killed over the two-decade insurgency.

description: An armed conflict in Bangladesh's Chittagong Hill Tracts from 1977 to 1997 between the government and the indigenous Jumma movement (PCJSS and its Shanti Bahini guerrillas) over autonomy and land rights. It ended with a 1997 peace accord after roughly 30,000 deaths.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Chittagong Hill Tracts conflict
UCDP Conflict Encyclopedia

name: Musket Wars

casualtyRange.source: Crosby (The Musket Wars) drawing on demographer Ian Pool
casualtyRange.notes: Most estimates center on ~20,000 killed between 1818 and the early 1830s; some analyses extend to 20,000–40,000 across the full period. Crosby/Pool estimate a further ~30,000 (possibly up to ~80,000) enslaved or displaced. Figures are scholarly estimates, not precise counts.

description: A series of as many as 3,000 intertribal Māori battles fought across New Zealand as iwi acquired European muskets, dramatically escalating the lethality of warfare and reshaping tribal boundaries. The conflicts caused mass casualties, enslavement, and migration before tapering off around 1840.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Musket Wars
Crosby, The Musket Wars (1999); Ian Pool demographic data

name: Flagstaff War

casualtyRange.source: Te Ara / NZ History compiled battle casualty figures
casualtyRange.notes: British and allied losses across Kororāreka, Puketutu, Ōhaeawai and Ruapekapeka totaled roughly 80–90 killed; Ngāpuhi losses (Heke/Kawiti) perhaps up to ~200 killed and wounded. No single authoritative total exists.

description: Also called the Northern War, fought between 11 March 1845 and 11 January 1846 around the Bay of Islands between Ngāpuhi led by Hōne Heke and Kawiti and British forces with allied Māori. It included the battles of Kororāreka, Puketutu, Ōhaeawai and the siege of Ruapekapeka Pā.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Flagstaff War
Te Ara Encyclopedia of New Zealand: Northern War 1845–1846

name: First Taranaki War
countries: Te Āti Awa and allied Māori

casualtyRange.source: Te Ara / standard NZ Wars accounts
casualtyRange.notes: Roughly 200 killed in total; precise Māori losses uncertain.

description: An armed conflict over disputed land sales at Waitara in the Taranaki district fought between Māori and the colonial government from March 1860 to March 1861. It marked a major escalation of the New Zealand Wars and ended in an inconclusive truce.

sources.label: Wikipedia: First Taranaki War
Te Ara Encyclopedia of New Zealand: New Zealand Wars

name: Invasion of the Waikato

casualtyRange.source: Te Ara / NZ History (Taranaki and Waikato campaigns combined ~1,800 Māori and ~800 European dead)
casualtyRange.notes: Combined Taranaki–Waikato campaign deaths are cited as about 1,800 Māori and 800 Europeans; the Waikato invasion itself accounts for a large but not separately quantified share. Range reflects the Waikato portion only.

description: A nine-month British military campaign (July 1863–April 1864) led by Lieutenant-General Duncan Cameron against the Māori King Movement, including the battles of Rangiriri and Ōrākau. Its outcome led to large-scale confiscation of Māori land in the Waikato.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Invasion of the Waikato
Te Ara Encyclopedia of New Zealand: New Zealand Wars

name: Tauranga campaign
countries: Ngāi Te Rangi and allied Māori

casualtyRange.notes: At Gate Pā British losses were 31 killed and 80 wounded; Māori losses ~25–30. At Te Ranga over 100 Māori were killed or fatally wounded. Total killed across the campaign roughly 150–200.

description: A six-month conflict in the Bay of Plenty in early 1864 between Ngāi Te Rangi and British forces, marked by the British defeat at Gate Pā (Pukehinahina) on 29 April and their decisive victory at Te Ranga in June. The campaign led to the confiscation of large tracts of Tauranga Māori land.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Tauranga campaign
NZ History (Manatū Taonga): Gate Pā

name: Second Taranaki War
countries: New Zealand Government and colonial forces
description: A period of hostilities in the Taranaki district from 1863 to 1866 driven by Māori resentment over the Waitara land dispute, large-scale land confiscation, and the rise of the Pai Mārire (Hauhau) movement. It involved sustained bush-clearing campaigns and Māori guerrilla resistance.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Second Taranaki War
NZ History (Manatū Taonga): The second Taranaki war

name: East Cape War
description: A series of conflicts fought on the east coast of the North Island from April 1865 to October 1866 between colonial and allied Māori forces and supporters of the Pai Mārire (Hauhau) movement. The fighting, including the siege of Waerenga-a-Hika, was driven by land confiscation and religious upheaval.

sources.label: Wikipedia: East Cape War
Te Ara Encyclopedia of New Zealand: New Zealand Wars

name: Te Kooti's War
countries: New Zealand Government and kūpapa Māori
description: A guerrilla campaign waged from 1868 to 1872 by the prophet-leader Te Kooti Arikirangi Te Turuki after escaping imprisonment on the Chatham Islands, including the 1868 Matawhero killings. Colonial and allied Māori forces pursued him for years before he escaped into the King Country.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Te Kooti's War
Te Ara Encyclopedia of New Zealand: New Zealand Wars

name: Wars of Hawaiian Unification
description: A series of campaigns from the 1780s to 1810 through which Kamehameha I conquered and unified the Hawaiian Islands, aided by European firearms and advisors. Key battles included Mokuʻōhai, Kepaniwai, and Nuʻuanu, with Kauaʻi ceded peacefully by 1810.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Unification of Hawaii
Kuykendall, The Hawaiian Kingdom vol. 1

name: Battle of Mokuʻōhai
description: Fought in 1782 in Kona on the island of Hawaiʻi, this was Kamehameha I's first major victory, in which his rival cousin Kīwalaʻō was killed. The battle left Kamehameha in control of much of the Big Island and launched his campaign of unification.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Mokuʻōhai
Kuykendall, The Hawaiian Kingdom vol. 1

name: Battle of Kepaniwai
description: Fought in 1790 in the ʻĪao Valley of Maui, where Kamehameha I's forces, using cannon, decisively defeated the Maui army of Kalanikūpule. The slaughter was so great that the stream was said to be dammed with bodies, giving the battle its name ('the damming of the waters').

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Kepaniwai
Kuykendall, The Hawaiian Kingdom vol. 1

name: Battle of Nuʻuanu

casualtyRange.source: Standard accounts (over 700 Oʻahu warriors driven off the pali)
casualtyRange.notes: More than 700 Oʻahu warriors were said to have been driven or to have jumped off the Nuʻuanu Pali; total deaths are uncertain. Figures are traditional estimates.

description: Fought in May 1795 on Oʻahu, the climactic battle of Kamehameha I's unification campaign, in which he defeated Kalanikūpule with an army of about 12,000 men. Hundreds of Oʻahu warriors were driven over the Nuʻuanu Pali cliff, after which Kamehameha's realm was first called the Kingdom of Hawaiʻi.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Nuʻuanu
Kuykendall, The Hawaiian Kingdom vol. 1

name: Tongan Civil War
countries: Tuʻi Kanokupolu and rival chiefly lines
description: A roughly fifty-year period of succession warfare that began with the murder of the Tuʻi Kanokupolu Tukuʻaho in 1799 and was worsened by the introduction of firearms. The wars ended with the triumph of Tāufaʻāhau, who unified Tonga and ruled as King George Tupou I from 1845.

sources.label: Wikipedia: History of Tonga
Campbell, Island Kingdom: Tonga Ancient and Modern

name: Burmese–Siamese War (1802–1805)
description: A war over the Lan Na city-states comprising the Burmese invasion of Chiang Mai in 1802 and the Siamese invasion and destruction of Chiang Saen in 1804. Chiang Saen was plundered and its roughly 23,000 inhabitants were deported and resettled across Siam and Laos.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Burmese–Siamese War (1802–1805)
Lieberman, Strange Parallels; standard Thai–Burmese historiography

name: Burmese–Siamese War (1809–1812)
description: Also called the Burmese Invasion of Thalang, this conflict centered on control of tin-rich Phuket Island (Thalang/Junk Ceylon) and the Andaman coast. The town of Thalang fell and was burned in January 1810; it was the last Burmese offensive into Siamese territory in Thai history.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Burmese–Siamese War (1809–1812)
Lieberman, Strange Parallels; standard Thai–Burmese historiography

name: Burmese–Siamese War (1849–1855)
description: Also called the Siamese Invasions of Kengtung, a series of Siamese and Lan Na expeditions against the Tai Khün state of Kengtung under Burmese suzerainty, aimed at gaining access to Chiang Hung (Sipsongpanna). Three invasions between 1850 and 1854 all failed, and the Siamese were driven back by 1855.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Burmese–Siamese War (1849–1855)
Lieberman, Strange Parallels; standard Thai–Burmese historiography

name: Battle of Rangiriri

casualtyRange.source: NZ History / Te Ara battle tallies
casualtyRange.notes: About 41 Māori killed (including six chiefs); British dead numbered 37 (two officers and 35 men), with ten of 93 wounded later dying. 183 Māori were taken prisoner. Combined deaths roughly 80–90.

description: Fought on 20 November 1863 during the Invasion of the Waikato, this assault on a Māori King Movement fortified line cost both sides more men than any other single engagement of the New Zealand Wars to that point. British troops took the position after Māori within surrendered, yielding 183 prisoners.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Rangiriri
NZ History (Manatū Taonga): Rangiriri

name: Battle of Ōrākau

casualtyRange.source: NZ History / Te Ara battle tallies
casualtyRange.notes: Up to about 160 Māori were killed, most during the breakout, plus 17 British regulars dead and 51 wounded. It was the single greatest loss of life of the wars.

description: Fought over three days in late March and early April 1864, the final major battle of the Waikato campaign, in which a heavily outnumbered Māori garrison made a defiant stand and breakout. It is the best-known engagement of the New Zealand Wars and inspired the films 'Rewi's Last Stand.'

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Ōrākau
Te Ara Encyclopedia of New Zealand: Waikato War major battles

name: Wairau Affray

casualtyRange.notes: 22 British settlers killed (nine after surrender) and 4 Māori killed, including Te Rongo, wife of Te Rangihaeata.

description: Also called the Wairau Massacre, this clash on 17 June 1843 in the Wairau Valley was the first serious armed confrontation between British settlers and Māori after the Treaty of Waitangi. A New Zealand Company survey party attempting to arrest Te Rauparaha and Te Rangihaeata was routed, with most settler deaths occurring after surrender.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Wairau Affray
NZ History (Manatū Taonga): The Wairau incident

name: Alauddin Khalji's Conquest of Ranthambore
description: In 1301 the Delhi Sultanate under Alauddin Khalji besieged and captured the Chahamana fortress of Ranthambore; King Hammira and his followers died fighting while the women performed jauhar (mass self-immolation).

sources.label: Wikipedia: Alauddin Khalji's conquest of Ranthambore
Banarsi Prasad Saksena / Kishori Saran Lal, History of the Khaljis

name: Siege of Warangal (1310)
description: Alauddin Khalji's general Malik Kafur besieged the Kakatiya capital Warangal in early 1310, forcing King Prataparudra to submit and pay enormous tribute, extending Delhi Sultanate suzerainty deep into the southern Deccan.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Siege of Warangal (1310)
Kishori Saran Lal, History of the Khaljis

name: Battle of Chausa
description: On 26 June 1539 the Afghan ruler Sher Shah Suri defeated the Mughal emperor Humayun near Chausa on the Ganges; Humayun barely escaped and Sher Shah proclaimed himself emperor.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Chausa
Britannica: Battle of Chausa

name: Battle of Kannauj
description: On 17 May 1540 Sher Shah Suri again routed Humayun near Kannauj (Bilgram), driving the Mughal emperor into a fifteen-year exile and establishing Sur dynasty rule over North India.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Kannauj
Jaques, Dictionary of Battles and Sieges

name: Siege of Chittorgarh (1567-1568)

casualtyRange.notes: Chronicle figure of ~30,000 civilians massacred after the fort fell on 23 Feb 1568; combat losses additional and unquantified.

description: Akbar's Mughal army besieged the Mewar stronghold of Chittorgarh from October 1567 to February 1568; after the fort fell Akbar ordered a massacre reported at around 30,000 civilians, breaking organized Rajput resistance to the Mughals.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Siege of Chittorgarh (1567-1568)
Abu'l-Fazl, Akbarnama

name: Battle of Samugarh
description: The decisive battle of the Mughal war of succession, fought 29 May 1658 near Agra, in which Aurangzeb defeated his elder brother and heir-apparent Dara Shikoh, opening Aurangzeb's path to the imperial throne.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Samugarh
Jadunath Sarkar, History of Aurangzib

name: Battle of Pratapgad
description: On 10 November 1659 Shivaji killed the Bijapur general Afzal Khan at a parley below Pratapgad fort and routed his army, the first major Maratha victory over a regional power and a foundational episode in Maratha ascendancy.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Pratapgarh
Jadunath Sarkar, Shivaji and His Times

name: Battle of Raichur
description: In 1520 Krishnadevaraya's Vijayanagara army defeated the Bijapur Sultanate at Raichur, capturing the contested Doab fortress and marking the high point of Vijayanagara military power in the Deccan.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Raichur
Robert Sewell, A Forgotten Empire (Vijayanagar)

name: Chola Conquest of Anuradhapura
description: Around 993 CE Rajaraja I's Chola army invaded northern Sri Lanka and sacked the ancient capital Anuradhapura, annexing the north as a Chola province and inaugurating roughly three-quarters of a century of Chola rule in the island.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Chola conquest of Anuradhapura
Nilakanta Sastri, The CoLas

name: Battle of Dhi Qar
description: An early-7th-century clash (commonly dated c. 609-611) in which the Arab Banu Bakr confederation defeated a Sasanian Persian expedition near Dhi Qar in southern Iraq, remembered as a symbolic blow to Persian prestige over the Arabs.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Dhi Qar
Encyclopaedia Iranica: Du Qar

name: Battle of Jalula
description: Fought in 637 northeast of the captured Sasanian capital Ctesiphon, the Rashidun army under Hashim ibn Utba routed the regrouped Persian forces at Jalula, clearing the route into the Iranian plateau during the Muslim conquest of Persia.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Jalula
Encyclopaedia Iranica: Jalula

name: Battle of Nahavand
description: Fought in 642 near Nahavand, the Rashidun army shattered the last major Sasanian field force under Yazdegerd III; called the 'Victory of Victories,' it ended organized Persian resistance to the Muslim conquest.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Nahavand
Britannica: Battle of Nahavand

name: Battle of the Camel
countries: Coalition of Aisha, Talha and Zubayr

casualtyRange.notes: Often-cited estimate of 10,000-15,000 dead, mostly on the rebel side; derived from medieval Arabic chronicles and not firmly verifiable.

description: Fought outside Basra in December 656 during the First Fitna, Caliph Ali defeated the rebellion of Aisha, Talha and Zubayr; Talha and Zubayr were killed, marking the first major battle of the first Islamic civil war.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of the Camel
Britannica: Battle of the Camel

name: Battle of Siffin

casualtyRange.notes: Chronicles report figures such as ~45,000 Syrian and ~25,000 Iraqi dead; these are unverifiable medieval estimates and likely inflated.

description: Fought in 657 on the banks of the Euphrates between Caliph Ali's Iraqi army and Mu'awiya's Syrian forces during the First Fitna, the indecisive battle ended in arbitration that weakened Ali and led toward the Umayyad Caliphate.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Siffin
Britannica: Battle of Siffin

name: Battle of Nahrawan
description: In July 658 Caliph Ali crushed the Kharijites, his former supporters who had broken with him after the Siffin arbitration, at the Nahrawan canal; the surviving Kharijite hostility led to Ali's assassination in 661.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Nahrawan
Britannica: Battle of Nahrawan

name: Battle of Karbala
description: On 10 October 680 an Umayyad army killed the Prophet's grandson Husayn ibn Ali and most of his small retinue at Karbala; the massacre triggered the Second Fitna and became the defining event of Shia Islam.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Karbala
Britannica: Battle of Karbala

name: Battle of Jam
description: In 1528 the teenage Safavid Shah Tahmasp I, using artillery and a wagon-laager, defeated an Uzbek army near Jam while relieving besieged Herat, checking Shaybanid expansion into Khorasan.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Tahmasp I
Roger Savory, Iran under the Safavids

name: Battle of Gulnabad

casualtyRange.notes: Safavid dead estimated between 5,000 and 15,000; Afghan losses an order of magnitude smaller.

description: On 8 March 1722 the Hotaki Afghan army under Mahmud Hotak decisively defeated a larger Safavid force at Gulnabad outside Isfahan, opening the way to the siege of the capital and the collapse of the Safavid dynasty.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Gulnabad
Michael Axworthy, The Sword of Persia

name: Siege of Isfahan (1722)

casualtyRange.notes: Tens of thousands of civilians (estimates up to ~80,000) died of starvation and disease during the six-month blockade; figures are contemporary estimates, not census data.

description: From March to October 1722 the Hotaki Afghan army blockaded the Safavid capital Isfahan; famine and disease killed tens of thousands of civilians before Shah Sultan Husayn surrendered, ending Safavid power in Iran.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Siege of Isfahan
Laurence Lockhart, The Fall of the Safavi Dynasty

name: Battle of Karnal

casualtyRange.notes: Mughal dead commonly estimated around 10,000 (some sources higher); Persian losses very light (~hundreds). Figures vary by source.

description: On 24 February 1739 Nader Shah's Afsharid Persian army crushed the much larger Mughal force under Muhammad Shah near Karnal within hours, opening the road to Delhi and accelerating the Mughal Empire's decline.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Karnal
Michael Axworthy, The Sword of Persia

name: Battle of Pollilur (1780)
description: On 10 September 1780, during the Second Anglo-Mysore War, Mysorean forces under Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan annihilated a British East India Company column under William Baillie near Pollilur, one of the Company's worst defeats in India and a notable use of iron-cased rockets.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Pollilur (1780)
Jaques, Dictionary of Battles and Sieges

name: Third Battle of Panipat

casualtyRange.notes: ~60,000-70,000 killed in the fighting; including the post-battle massacre of prisoners and non-combatants, Shejwalkar estimates up to ~100,000 Maratha dead. Heavily disputed.

description: On 14 January 1761 the Durrani Afghan army under Ahmad Shah Durrani defeated the Maratha Empire at Panipat in one of the largest and bloodiest 18th-century battles; massive Maratha losses checked their northern expansion and reshaped the Indian balance of power.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Third Battle of Panipat
T.S. Shejwalkar, Panipat 1761

name: Battle of Kharda
description: Fought in 1795, the Battle of Kharda was the last major engagement in which the united Maratha Confederacy decisively defeated the Nizam of Hyderabad, marking a high point of Maratha power before its later fragmentation.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Kharda
Stewart Gordon, The Marathas 1600-1818

name: Battle of Aslanduz
description: On 31 October-1 November 1812, during the Russo-Persian War of 1804-1813, a Russian force under Pyotr Kotlyarevsky launched a surprise night attack and routed Abbas Mirza's Persian army at Aslanduz on the Aras, hastening the Treaty of Gulistan.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Aslanduz
Russo-Persian War (1804-1813), Wikipedia

name: Battle of Ganja (1826)
description: In autumn 1826, during the Russo-Persian War of 1826-1828, Russian forces defeated Abbas Mirza's Qajar army near Ganja, ending Persian hopes of reversing earlier losses in the Caucasus and leading toward the Treaty of Turkmenchay.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Battle of Ganja (1826)

name: First Herat War
description: From November 1837 the Qajar shah Mohammad Mirza besieged Herat, defended by Kamran Shah and Yar Mohammad Khan; British pressure and a naval threat in the Gulf forced Persia to lift the siege in September 1838, a key episode of the Great Game.

sources.label: Wikipedia: First Herat War

name: Siege of Baghdad (1638)
description: Sultan Murad IV personally led the Ottoman army that besieged and recaptured Baghdad from the Safavids over 15 November-25 December 1638; the victory led to the 1639 Treaty of Zuhab, fixing the lasting Ottoman-Iranian frontier in Iraq.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Siege of Baghdad (1638)

name: Battle of Sobraon

casualtyRange.notes: Sikh dead and wounded commonly given as ~8,000-10,000, many drowned when the bridge of boats collapsed; British/Bengal losses ~2,283.
